Needs draft copy

Output edited copy with a reading-level score and an edit log

Used by CREA-W01, CREA-W02, CREA-W05, CREA-W06

SKILL.md
---
name: compliance/copy-craft-rules
owner: crea-paid-creative-copy
version: 1
invoke_when: any drafted copy needs the account's fixed writing rules applied,
  before the separate claim-tier check
inputs: draft copy
outputs: edited copy, reading-level score, edit log
---
Purpose: apply the same fixed craft rules to every draft regardless of which
skill wrote it, so voice and readability never drift by writer or by format.

Steps
1. Score reading level in code (not by eye) and rewrite until the draft
   clears the grade-10 target; a draft that reads clever but tests at grade
   13 gets simplified, not defended.
2. Check single-idea discipline: exactly one dominant appeal and exactly one
   CTA per asset, unless the approved idea explicitly calls for testing two
   in the same piece.
3. Order proof points from strongest real evidence to weakest, cutting any
   proof point with nothing behind it rather than padding the count.
4. Cut every em dash, every inflated or vague superlative with no fact
   behind it, and any phrasing that reads as generically AI-written rather
   than in the brand's real voice.
5. Replace spelled-out numbers with digits throughout.

Checks: grade-10 or below; single idea and single CTA; no em dash; digits,
not spelled-out numbers.

Output: the edited copy, its reading-grade score, and a short edit log
naming what changed and why.

Example: "we're absolutely thrilled to introduce an incredible new way to
elevate your morning" becomes "start your morning with 2 minutes of real
energy, no crash."

Steps

   account's own historical curve for that format, not a generic industry
   benchmark.

   declining CTR alongside reach that is still growing points to a
   targeting or sequencing issue, not creative wear-out.
3. Split the cause explicitly: audience-pool exhaustion or genuine creative
   fatigue, naming the specific number that decided it.
4. For a creative cause, name the specific part that wore out, the hook, the
   visual, or the whole concept, rather than a general "this ad is tired"
   verdict with nothing actionable in it.

Purpose: write the lines that build trust in how an order gets paid for and
delivered, using only real incentives and real carrier facts, since this
messaging often touches checkout trust directly. For a COD brand this
includes the India-market option of moving a cash-on-delivery buyer toward
prepaid and lowering the risk of a return-to-origin (RTO); that option

   pull the COD share and RTO rate.

   option, a card or wallet trust fact, or, for a COD brand, a real discount
   amount or a real faster-dispatch promise, never a vague "pay online for a

   delivery window, and a real tracking or call-before-delivery fact if
   that is actually offered.

   since a delivery-time, BNPL or discount claim here is a common source of
   drift between what marketing promises and what ops can do.

    name: meta-concept
    owner: media-buyer

    ---
    Purpose: turn one tested idea into one correctly built Meta ad set: broad,
    excluded from existing customers, with clean placements and enough ads to be
    read fairly.

    Steps
    1. Define the concept: one SKU, one pain point, one offer. Any change to one of
       these starts a new ad set, not an edit to this one.
    2. Check for persona overlap with a live ad set; keep non-overlapping personas
       apart.

       targeting logic in the creative, not the settings. Cap any interest or
       lookalike test as a small, labelled sandbox.
    4. Exclude existing customers, sized to the repurchase cycle.
    5. Turn off weak placements and every automatic creative edit on product ads.
    6. Pick CBO by default (ABO only at high AOV, low volume); set any cap at ad
       set level.
    7. Load 2-6 exposures worth of ads (minimum 3: the concept ad plus 3 hooks).
    8. Pass the built ad set to the pre-launch QA skill before it goes live.

    - One SKU, one pain point, one offer per ad set.
    - Existing customers excluded; broad targeting used; sandbox tests labelled and
      capped.

    one new ad set, broad cold, commuter-persona exclusion of existing buyers,

Needs brand brain: catalogue, margin, brand terms, audit: MEDIA-C02 output

Used by MEDIA-W20

SKILL.md
---
    name: google-architecture
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: new account, an audit flags structure, or the monthly brand check is due
    inputs: catalogue, margin, brand terms, prior audit
    outputs: architecture diagram, brand/non-brand split plan, change list
    ---
    Purpose: give every Google campaign one job, and make sure brand-name traffic
    never gets counted as growth.

    Steps
    1. Map every campaign to one funnel job; flag any overlap.
    2. Default to one campaign per job; a second campaign for the same job needs a
       written reason.
    3. One campaign per country; never mix locations inside one PMax.
    4. Set safe defaults on anything new: Sales objective, Purchase-only goal,
       Search Partners and Display off, Presence targeting, tablets/TV off.
    5. Split brand from non-brand everywhere it can run: Search, Shopping, PMax.
    6. Exclude brand from cold campaigns with a negative list AND an audience
       exclusion, not just one of the two.
    7. Put brand on manual bidding or impression share at a higher ROAS target;
       check impression share actually covers the brand name.
    8. Scan cold-campaign search terms monthly for brand leakage; merge orphan
       campaigns into the account's real structure.

    Checks
    - Every campaign traces to one job and, if extra, a written reason.
    - No brand traffic inflates the non-brand growth number.

    Output: architecture diagram, split plan, change list.

    Example: a PMax campaign is running for both the US and Canada -> split into two
    country campaigns with a written reason (currency and duty messaging differ).

    - No new SKU diluted the proven bestseller group's data.

SKILL.md
---
    name: meta-test-sizing
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a new Meta creative test is ready to size
    inputs: target CPA, purchase cycle, planned test budget
    outputs: test brief, kill-rule sheet
    ---
    Purpose: size a Meta creative test so its result can actually be trusted,
    instead of leaning on the platform's own learning-phase suggestion.

    Steps
    1. Compute the test budget: target conversions x CPA / test days, in code.
    2. Set the kill-rule threshold: 3-5x target CPA before any judgement.
    3. Set the read window to match the purchase cycle; never under 5 days below
       $50k/month spend.

       that window; if not, raise the budget or extend the window before launch.
    5. Never allow a same-day or $1-2-spend kill call.

    Checks
    - The budget came from the formula, not Meta's 50-conversions rule.
    - The ad set can mathematically reach its read threshold in the window given.

    Output: a test brief (budget, read window, kill rule) for the launch.

    Example: target CPA is $20, target 15 conversions to judge, test runs 5 days ->
    budget = 15 x $20 / 5 = $60/day.
media/pace-budget/google Google bid stage and budget pacing platform=google, task=bid_and_budget

Invoke when the weekly Google bid or budget review is due

Needs metric contract: cpc, roas_blended, cpa, spend, aov, connector: google ads (manual)

Output bid stage plan + budget plan + pacing log

Used by MEDIA-W24

SKILL.md
---
    name: google-bid-budget
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: the weekly Google bid or budget review is due
    inputs: CPC, CPA, AOV, spend, current bid strategy
    outputs: bid stage plan, budget plan, pacing log
    ---
    Purpose: move Google bidding and budget forward in small, reversible steps
    tied to the brand's own break-even math, never a platform default or a big
    jump.

    Steps
    1. Cap a new account's bids at break-even CPA / conversion rate.
    2. Move to Maximize Conversion Value once conversions arrive; add Target ROAS
       only once volume supports it, set near the actual number.
    3. Size Shopping/Search launch budgets at 3-4x AOV/day; PMax at $50-100/day and
       3x non-brand CPA.
    4. Raise budgets in small weekly steps; cut faster than you raise.
    5. Treat "limited by budget" as a signal to test, not an automatic raise.
    6. Step bid targets gently; use an aggressive cut, not a timid one, to break a
       Target ROAS death spiral.

    Checks
    - No budget doubled or target halved in a single step.
    - Every cap traces to the brand's own break-even math.

    Output: bid stage plan, budget plan, pacing log.

    Example: account shows "limited by budget" on a campaign at 1.5x target ROAS ->
    treated as a signal to test a modest raise, not proof to double the budget.

    inputs: spend, orders, revenue, trailing 14-day history
    outputs: daily read, weekly read, anomaly alert, spend forecast
    ---
    Purpose: give the founder one page a day and one a week on what is spent, what
    it returned, what moved sharply, and where the month is headed, all computed
    in code.

    Steps
    1. Blend spend, orders and revenue into MER in code.
    2. Compute the trailing 14-day median for spend and ROAS; flag days 50%+ off
       it.

       the 3 ads that moved most.

    7. Mark any missing platform or day as unavailable, never zero.

    Checks
    - Every number traces to code, never model arithmetic.
    - No computed 0 hides a genuinely missing data point.

    Output: daily read, weekly read, anomaly alert, spend forecast.

    Example: ROAS drops 60% against the 14-day median on a Tuesday -> check CAPI
    health first; a dropped event, not bidding, explains the drop.

Used by MEDIA-W27 · shared with prod

SKILL.md
---
    name: marketplace-read
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a marketplace or rapid-delivery/grocery spend read is due (India only: quick-commerce)
    inputs: seller dashboard export, SKU landed cost, ad console export
    outputs: contribution margin report, ACOS/TACOS read
    ---
    Purpose: read marketplace and rapid-delivery/grocery ad results on the real
    number, since platform dashboards inflate ROAS 30-50% by pricing at list price
    (MRP, India) instead of transaction value.

    Steps
    1. Recompute ROAS on actual transaction value, net of platform commission
       (15-25%) and applicable US sales tax on the commission (GST, India only).
    2. Add inwarding fees, storage cost and a 2-5% list-price write-off budget for
       damage/expiry.
    3. Calculate the weekly per-fulfillment-center order volume needed to clear the
       55-60% gross margin floor (per-dark-store, India only).
    4. Flag whether a shortfall is a volume problem (more orders fixes it) or a
       structural one (needs repricing or a COGS cut).
    5. Read Amazon/Walmart/Target ACOS or TACOS against the SKU's own margin
       (Flipkart, India only).

    Checks
    - No ROAS number in the report is based on list price (MRP, India only).
    - Every margin flag names whether it is volume or structural.

    Output: contribution margin report, ACOS/TACOS read.

    Example: platform dashboard shows 4.2x ROAS; recomputed on transaction value
    net of commission and fees it is 2.6x -> the true number the SKU is judged on.

---
    name: peak-sale-ramp

    before the sale starts, instead of reacting during it.

    - The ramp plan was checked against stock, not assumed.

Output test brief + read point and result writeup + registry entry

Used by MEDIA-W12

SKILL.md
---
    name: incrementality-test
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: platform ROAS and blended MER disagree after attribution is tightened
    inputs: ROAS, spend, geographic sales spread
    outputs: test brief, result writeup, registry entry
    ---
    Purpose: find out whether disputed spend is buying orders that would not have
    happened anyway, only after cheaper fixes (attribution, reconciliation) are
    already done.

    Steps
    1. Confirm attribution is already tightened and reconciled; this test is not a
       substitute for that work.
    2. Pick the test type: Meta Conversion Lift, geo holdout, or matched-market
       geo test.
    3. Size the split, minimum spend and read window.
    4. Write the brief: hypothesis, holdout design, read point, proof bar.
    5. Read the result; update the brand's own effect prior for that spend level.
    6. Feed the result into budget decisions; never let it change bidding directly.

    Checks
    - Reconciliation happened first; the test is not a first resort.
    - The result is logged to the registry, win or lose.

    Output: test brief, result writeup, registry entry.

    Example: Meta shows 4x ROAS but blended MER shows 1.8x even after
    reconciliation -> a geo holdout is sized to find the real incremental lift.

---
    name: trafficking-qa
    owner: media-buyer

    invoke_when: any campaign, ad set or ad on any platform is about to go live
    inputs: the built campaign, the approved plan, platform creative specs
    outputs: a pass/fail QA checklist

    Purpose: run the same fixed check an ad ops trafficker runs by hand before any
    launch, on any platform, so a known gap never goes live by accident.

    1. Confirm the conversion event and pixel/CAPI fire on the exact landing page

    - Every item on the list has a pass or fail, not a skip.
    - A failed check held the launch, with no exception.

    launch held, one-line fix requested before it goes live.

media/partnerships/affiliate-program Affiliate and creator partner program management job=affiliate_program

Invoke when a new affiliate application arrives, the weekly program health check is due, or affiliate/coupon activity needs a fraud scan

Needs applicant profile and traffic source, brand's affiliate policy and commission terms, affiliate network data

Output approve/reject decisions with reasons + onboarding kit + dormant-affiliate list + leaderboard + fraud flag list with evidence

Used by MEDIA-W25

SKILL.md
---
    name: affiliate-program
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a new application arrives, the weekly health check is due, or fraud needs a scan
    inputs: applicant profile, affiliate policy, network click/conversion logs
    outputs: approve/reject decisions, onboarding kit, dormant list, fraud flags
    ---
    Purpose: run the affiliate program the way an affiliate manager would, without
    a human touching every routine application, while catching the fraud patterns
    that steal commission without earning it.

    Steps
    1. Screen each application against a fixed rule set: site quality, traffic
       source, category fit, prior brand mentions.
    2. Auto-approve a clear pass, auto-reject clear spam, route only the borderline
       case to the founder.
    3. Generate the approved affiliate's link, coupon code and starter asset kit.
    4. Flag any affiliate with no clicks or sales in 60 days.
    5. Watch for fraud signatures: too-fast click-to-conversion, data-centre or
       proxy ISP traffic, the brand's coupon codes on public aggregator sites
       without rights, or an affiliate bidding on the brand name.
    6. Hold commission on any flagged conversion pending founder review; never
       auto-pay a flagged one.

    Checks
    - Only borderline applications reached the founder.
    - Every held commission has evidence attached, not a hunch.

    Output: approve/reject decisions, onboarding kit, dormant list, leaderboard,
    fraud flag list.

    Example: a conversion completes 40 seconds after the click, from a data-centre
    IP -> flagged, commission held, founder notified before payout.

Used by MEDIA-W29

SKILL.md
---
    name: policy-appeals
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: a new disapproval lands or the daily account-quality check is due
    inputs: disapproval reasons, account-quality dashboards, claim tiers
    outputs: rejection log, appeal drafts, account-quality trend flag
    ---
    Purpose: treat every ad rejection as a diagnosable policy-clause problem with a
    named fix, instead of a one-off surprise, and catch an account-quality slide
    before it becomes a restriction.

    Steps
    1. Pull every disapproved ad and its stated reason daily.
    2. Map the reason to the exact policy clause and the likely real cause: claim,
       image text ratio, restricted-category wording, or landing page mismatch.
    3. Propose the smallest edit that clears the violation without changing the
       offer or claim tier.
    4. Draft an appeal only for a rejection believed wrongly applied; a human
       submits it.
    5. Watch the account-quality score for a downward trend and flag it early.
    6. Log rejection reasons by category to catch a repeating pattern.

    Checks
    - Every rejection has a named clause and a proposed fix.
    - No appeal is submitted without a human review of the draft.

    Output: rejection log, appeal drafts, account-quality trend flag.

    Example: 4 ads in one week rejected for the same "before/after" claim wording
    -> pattern logged, a claim-tier fix proposed once instead of firefighting each
    ad separately.

    2. Shortlist DSPs or surfaces by real fit to the brand's category and data,
       not by trend.

    4. Set stop and scale thresholds before the pilot starts.

       creative pipeline.

       platform's benchmarks.

    - Saturation was confirmed with data, not assumed.

    Output: go/no-go recommendation, pilot test plan.

    -> a small, capped Criteo pilot is sized and read against the brand's own CAC
    target, not Criteo's benchmark.

Invoke when the brand's kill/keep/scale and bid thresholds are established and ready to standardise

Needs existing kill/keep/scale thresholds, platform automation/rule-engine capability

Used by MEDIA-W30

SKILL.md
---
    name: rule-automation
    owner: media-buyer
    version: 1
    invoke_when: kill/keep/scale and bid thresholds are established and ready to standardise
    inputs: existing thresholds, platform automation capability
    outputs: documented rule set, firing log
    ---
    Purpose: turn thresholds the brand already uses by hand into standing,
    auditable automations, never a new rule invented on the spot, and never live
    until the founder switches writes on.

    Steps
    1. Translate each existing threshold into an explicit if-then rule per
       platform.
    2. Keep the rule set consistent across Meta, Google and TikTok, adapting only
       for each platform's own automation options.
    3. Log every firing with the before and after state.
    4. Auto-pause a rule that fires far more than expected; that usually means
       tracking broke, not that the rule found real signal.
    5. Hold every rule inactive on a surface until the founder switches writes on
       for it.

    Checks
    - Every rule traces to a threshold already approved elsewhere, not a new one.
    - No rule is live on a surface without writes switched on.

    Output: documented rule set, firing log.

    Example: the existing kill rule (3-5x target CPA) becomes an if-then rule that
    pauses an ad set at 4x CPA and logs the before/after spend -- but stays
    dormant until Meta writes are switched on.

name: build-flow
owner: LIFE

invoke_when: an approved idea or a scheduled maintenance job calls for a new or rebuilt lifecycle flow
inputs: approved idea/trigger, brand brain, order/event history, registry
outputs: flow brief in the fixed output-contract shape
---
# Build a lifecycle flow

## Purpose
One procedure runs every flow build. The flow type picks the sub-skill; the shape of the
job (confirm trigger, set filters, map steps, draft copy, check discount, assemble brief)
never changes.

## Steps
1. Read the idea or trigger and name the flow type (welcome, browse-cart-abandon,
   post-purchase, win-back, sunset, back-in-stock, replenishment, loyalty-vip).
2. Load the matching sub-skill for that type; it owns the timing and content logic.
3. Confirm the trigger event actually fires in this store's data before building around it.
4. Set entry, exit and re-entry filters against every other live flow.
5. Map delay, channel and purpose per step using the sub-skill's rule.
6. Draft copy per step and channel via life/message; claim-check every step.
7. Set discount eligibility, if any, via life/discount-policy-check.
8. Assemble the flow brief and run the LIFE self-QA checklist.

## Checks
Trigger confirmed. No stage overlap with another flow. Every claim checked. Output
matches the flow-brief shape exactly.

## Output
A flow brief ready for the founder gate, plus the registry stub for the read point.

## Example
Idea: "Win-back flow underperforms; rebuild timing off purchase cadence." Output: a
3-email, 2-SMS win-back brief entering at 1.5x the customer's own average order gap,
exiting on purchase, no discount until email 3, read point 45 days post-launch.

# Welcome flow

## Purpose
Owns the timing and content logic specific to the welcome flow type, called by the
parent life/build-flow skill once the trigger is confirmed.

## Steps
1. Confirm the welcome trigger fires from real store data.
2. Apply the timing rule: front-loaded into the first 72 hours from signup, using the pop-up offer if one exists.
3. Set content focus per step: brand story, best-sellers, social proof, then the offer reminder with any urgency honestly framed.
4. Flag where a discount could sit, for life/discount-policy-check to clear.
5. Hand the step list back to life/build-flow for copy drafting and assembly.

## Checks
Trigger is real and recent. Timing matches this type's own rule. Content matches the
customer's actual state at this point, not a generic template.

## Output
Step list: {delay, channel, purpose} per step.

## Example
Signup at 10am Monday. Email 1 at signup (welcome, offer), email 2 at +24h (best-sellers), SMS at +48h (offer reminder), email 3 at +72h (last call on the offer, real deadline).

# Browse and cart/checkout abandonment flow

## Purpose
Owns the timing and content logic specific to the browse-cart-abandon flow type, called by the
parent life/build-flow skill once the trigger is confirmed.

## Steps
1. Confirm the browse-cart-abandon trigger fires from real store data.
2. Apply the timing rule: browse abandon starts 1-3 hours after a product view with no add-to-cart; cart/checkout abandon starts 30-60 minutes after cart or checkout start with no order.
3. Set content focus per step: browse abandon reads as a shop-assistant follow-up, not a hard sell; cart/checkout abandon uses dynamic product blocks and holds any discount back to a later step, never the first message.
4. Flag where a discount could sit, for life/discount-policy-check to clear.
5. Hand the step list back to life/build-flow for copy drafting and assembly.

## Checks
Trigger is real and recent. Timing matches this type's own rule. Content matches the
customer's actual state at this point, not a generic template.

## Output
Step list: {delay, channel, purpose} per step.

## Example
Cart abandoned at 3:15pm. SMS at +1h (no discount, just a reminder with the product), email at +4h (dynamic cart block, still no discount), email at +24h (discount appears for the first time, framed against a real reason to buy now).

# Win-back flow

## Purpose
Owns the timing and content logic specific to the win-back flow type, called by the
parent life/build-flow skill once the trigger is confirmed.

## Steps
1. Confirm the win-back trigger fires from real store data.
2. Apply the timing rule: starts when a customer passes 1.5x to 2x their own average order gap, not a flat day count for every brand.
3. Set content focus per step: leads with genuine value or news, not a discount, unless the customer's lapse cause is engagement decay with no other signal; a delivery-failure-caused lapse (return-to-sender, or RTO for India) routes to the trust-rebuild variant instead (see LIFE-W12).
4. Flag where a discount could sit, for life/discount-policy-check to clear.
5. Hand the step list back to life/build-flow for copy drafting and assembly.

## Checks
Trigger is real and recent. Timing matches this type's own rule. Content matches the
customer's actual state at this point, not a generic template.

## Output
Step list: {delay, channel, purpose} per step.

## Example
Customer's average gap is 40 days; no order at day 65 triggers entry. Email 1 (what's new, no discount), SMS at +5 days (soft nudge), email 2 at +10 days (matched offer sized to the customer's own value).

# Replenishment and subscription lifecycle messaging

## Purpose
Owns the timing and content logic specific to the replenishment flow type, called by the
parent life/build-flow skill once the trigger is confirmed.

## Steps
1. Confirm the replenishment trigger fires from real store data.
2. Apply the timing rule: timed to the product's real use-up cycle for replenishment reminders, and to the actual charge date for subscription messages; use predictive per-customer timing where enough order history exists, falling back to the fixed cycle otherwise.
3. Set content focus per step: replenishment reminders are practical and low-pressure; subscription messages state the charge date, amount and easy pause/skip link plainly, no fine print.
4. Flag where a discount could sit, for life/discount-policy-check to clear.
5. Hand the step list back to life/build-flow for copy drafting and assembly.

## Checks
Trigger is real and recent. Timing matches this type's own rule. Content matches the
customer's actual state at this point, not a generic template.

Step list: {delay, channel, purpose} per step.

Product use-up cycle is 30 days. Reminder at day 25 (before running out), a subscription charge reminder 3 days before the card is charged, with a one-tap skip link.

# Draft channel message copy

## Purpose
One drafting procedure, channel picked by select_by. Keeps subject/preview/body rules
for email separate from the character and consent rules for SMS (the default second
channel) and WhatsApp (a market option for India, EU, LATAM).

## Steps
1. Read the brief's purpose, audience and any discount/urgency rule.
2. Load the matching life/message/<channel> sub-skill.
3. Draft at or below tenth-grade reading level, in the brand's voice.
4. Hold discount mentions to the brief's specified position.
5. Cite every factual claim to a brand-record field.
6. Return the draft, flagged for shared/claim-check before it ships anywhere.

## Checks
Reading level under grade 10. No invented number or claim. Channel format matches
the sub-skill's rule (email has subject/preview lines; SMS/WhatsApp do not).

## Output
Draft copy per channel, claims cited, marked as a draft for human edit.

## Example
Brief: cart-abandon step 1, SMS, no discount. Output: "Still thinking about the Aria
necklace? It's saved in your cart. [link]" - short, no discount, one link, consent
footer per policy.

# Email message drafting

## Purpose
Writes the email-specific fields a flow or campaign step needs: subject line,
preview text, body and CTA, none of which SMS or WhatsApp carry, and flags any
spam-trigger language before the draft reaches life/deliverability-audit. Email
is still the channel that carries the most product detail and dynamic content, so
this skill also marks where a dynamic block (cart contents, recommended products)
belongs for the build step that follows.

## Steps
1. Write the subject line and the preview text as two separate, complementary
   lines; the preview should add information, not repeat the subject.
2. Write the body at a skimmable length with exactly one clear call to action,
   never two competing links fighting for the same click.
3. Mark where a dynamic product block or personalised image belongs, so the
   email-build step can wire it correctly.
4. Screen the subject line for spam-trigger words, ALL-CAPS and excess
   punctuation before handing the draft on.

## Checks
Subject and preview are both written, never left blank. Exactly one CTA per
email. No unscreened spam-trigger language reaches the build step.

## Output
{subject, preview, body, cta, dynamic_block_ref}

## Example
Subject: "Your Aria necklace is still here." Preview: "Free shipping ends
tonight." Body: three short lines, one button reading "Finish my order," with a
dynamic_block_ref pointing at the customer's actual saved cart.

# SMS message drafting

## Purpose
The default second channel after email, with US TCPA consent and quiet hours by
default and the equivalent local law elsewhere (see life/consent-governance). Writes
short, compliant SMS copy for a flow or campaign step: brand name up
front, a single link, and the opt-out instruction consent-governance requires,
all inside the quiet-hours window and cadence cap life/channel-policy has
already set for this brand and market. SMS earns its place through urgency and
brevity, not through carrying the same content an email already sent.

## Steps
1. Draft the message inside a carrier-friendly character length, with one link
   at most; a second link splits attention and often breaks link shortening.
2. Put the brand name at the very start of the message and add the opt-out
   instruction at the end, per the consent-governance rule for this market.
3. Check the scheduled send time against the quiet-hours window and the
   per-customer weekly cadence cap before it is queued.
4. Cut any factual claim that cannot be stated accurately inside the space
   available, rather than compressing it into something misleading.

## Checks
Opt-out instruction is present on every send. Quiet hours are respected for the
recipient's own market. Exactly one link appears in the message.

## Output
{body, link, opt_out_line}

## Example
"[Brand] Still want the Aria necklace? Your cart's saved: [link]. Reply STOP to
opt out." - one link, brand-first, opt-out included, sent inside quiet hours.

## Purpose

messages, and designs the reply-inviting opener for two-way conversations. WhatsApp is
a market option (common in India, EU and LATAM) where reach beats SMS and email; SMS
is the default second channel (see life/message/sms).

   around one that is missing or rejected.
2. Fill the template's variable slots, or write a free-form opener if the customer

4. Name the point at which a real reply hands off to a human agent.

# Lifecycle program audit

## Purpose
Scores flow and segmentation health against the standard set of 8 flow types and
produces a ranked backlog, so build sequencing is a read of real gaps, not a guess
at what "should" exist.

## Steps
1. List the 8 standard flow types and check each one's existence and health in the
   ESP: trigger fires, filters set, no stage overlap with another flow.
2. Pull flow-vs-campaign revenue split from the metric contract for context.
3. Flag every missing flow and every broken filter or overlap by name.
4. Rank the resulting gaps, plus any segmentation or deliverability flag, by
   expected revenue impact using order volume and AOV as the size input, computed
   in code.

## Checks
Every flow type in the standard set gets a row, even "missing." Every score traces
to a metric-contract field or an ESP read. No arithmetic done in the model.

## Output
A ranked backlog (for W01) or a monthly scorecard (for W11), both with the score
parts visible.

## Example
"Win-back flow: exists but no re-entry rule - claims same customer as sunset flow.
Ranked #2 behind 'no post-purchase flow exists' (#1, larger revenue gap)."

# On-site capture pop-up design

## Purpose
Designs the sign-up pop-up (offer, fields, trigger timing, targeting, layout) and
queues the test order, judged by what the sign-up is worth over time, not the
opt-in rate alone.

## Steps
1. Choose the offer type (percent, flat, gift, non-discount hook) from margin and
   discount policy, before any copy is written.
2. Set the minimum fields to capture, the trigger (time, scroll, exit-intent) and
   exclusions (existing subscribers, checkout page).
3. Draft mobile and desktop copy variants at a skimmable reading level.
4. Sequence the test queue: offer type first, then copy, then design, one variable
   at a time, versus the current control.

## Checks
No hidden or hard-to-find close button. Exclusions cover existing subscribers.
Judged by full-site conversion and list value per visitor, not opt-in rate.

## Output
Pop-up spec (offer, fields, trigger, targeting, copy) plus a sequenced test queue.

## Example
"Offer: free shipping over reference threshold, not 10% off (protects margin).
Trigger: exit-intent, desktop only. Test 1: this offer vs current 10%-off control."

# Consent, quiet hours and unsubscribe governance

## Purpose
Keeps every send legal by market: the right opt-in model, the right quiet-hours
window in local time, and an unsubscribe that is honoured immediately.

## Steps
1. List markets from real shipping/billing geography, not assumptions.
2. Research the opt-in model, record-keeping rule and quiet-hours window per market,
   with source and date.
3. Compare current ESP/SMS/WhatsApp consent fields against each market's rule and
   list every gap by name.
4. Set the quiet-hours schedule in local time per market and channel.
5. Set the unsubscribe/STOP SLA at or above the strictest applicable market law.

## Checks
Every legal claim has a URL and date. Quiet hours use local time, not the brand's
home timezone. Unsubscribe SLA meets or beats the legal minimum.

## Output
A consent rule set, a quiet-hours table, and an unsubscribe SLA, each per market.

## Example
"US: TCPA needs prior express written consent for SMS marketing; quiet hours
8am-9pm recipient local time. India: DPDP Act needs affirmative opt-in for WhatsApp
marketing; quiet hours 9pm-9am IST for SMS. Gap: current form has no separate
WhatsApp consent checkbox."

# Segment build

## Purpose
Builds and documents every standing segment (RFM tiers, buyer stage, VIP, win-back-
potential, high-potential, location, engaged audience) so flows and campaigns pull
from one shared, current definition instead of a one-off list.

## Steps
1. Score RFM tiers and buyer stage from order recency/frequency/monetary data, in
   code, against a fixed threshold script.
2. Score win-back-potential against the customer's own historical order gap, not a
   flat day count; score high-potential from early LTV-matching traits.
3. Build the location segment from shipping address, not billing.
4. Cross-check every segment against the flows/campaigns that use it.
5. Write the segment definition and push the refreshed membership to the ESP.

## Checks
All scoring in code. Every segment cites the real fields behind it. No segment is
referenced by a flow that no longer exists, or vice versa.

{name, logic (AND/OR, cited fields), expected_size, refresh_cadence, used_by}

# Deliverability and list-hygiene audit

## Purpose
Monitors sender reputation and inbox placement, keeps the list clean, and runs the
repair ladder in the right order when a figure degrades, treating content quality
as the first fix, not authentication settings.

## Steps
1. Pull domain/IP reputation, bounce and spam-complaint rates, and the unengaged
   list share for the week, from the ESP's own reported numbers.
2. Compare against the brand's own trailing 8-week baseline first.
3. If degraded, diagnose content (subject lines, spam-trigger words, image-to-text
   ratio) before touching sending infrastructure.
4. Run the repair ladder in order: fix content, pause to the most unengaged
   segment, suppress or re-permission chronic non-openers, check authentication
   (SPF/DKIM/DMARC) only if earlier steps do not explain it.
5. Update suppression per the standing hygiene policy.

## Checks
Content checked before infrastructure. No recent purchaser (last 90 days) suppressed
without a specific, named reason.

## Output
Weekly health report plus a repair-ladder log of steps taken and pending.

## Example
"Complaint rate up 0.1pt vs baseline. Cause: last Tuesday's subject line flagged
2 spam-trigger words. Fix: rewrite subject rule; no infrastructure change needed."

# Channel policy: SMS, WhatsApp and push

## Purpose
Sets what each non-email channel is for, how often it sends and what it costs to
run, so channels do not duplicate the same message to the same customer.

## Steps
1. Pull real per-message cost and volume for SMS, WhatsApp and push.
2. Check consent coverage per channel; a channel below its market's legal
   threshold is flagged before any cadence policy is set.
3. Assign content scope per channel (SMS: time-sensitive short offers and order
   updates by default; WhatsApp: order updates and high-value recovery where used,
   common in India, EU or LATAM; push: on-site nudges).
4. Set a per-customer weekly cadence cap and a monthly spend cap, sized to the
   real cost data.
5. Where SMS cost per send is high relative to WhatsApp (common in India, EU or
   LATAM), recommend shifting eligible message types, contingent on WhatsApp consent
   and template approval.

## Checks
Caps sized from real cost data, not a round number. No message type duplicated
across two channels to the same customer at once.

## Output
A channel policy document: content scope, cadence caps, cost caps, and any
recommended channel swap.

## Example
"SMS costs 3x WhatsApp per send in India. Move order-update messages to WhatsApp;
keep flash-sale urgency on SMS where WhatsApp template approval would be too slow."

# WhatsApp commerce program for India

## Purpose
Builds the India-specific WhatsApp program: cart recovery, order updates, a costed
COD-to-prepaid nudge, and automatic NDR recovery, where WhatsApp reach beats SMS
and email for Indian buyers.

## Steps
1. Pull COD share, RTO rate and cart abandonment scoped to Indian shipping
   addresses only, never blended with other markets.
2. Build the cart-recovery sequence using life/build-flow/browse-cart-abandon with
   WhatsApp as the lead channel.
3. Set order-update messages against real order-status events.
4. Size the COD-to-prepaid incentive against the RTO cost it measurably avoids.
5. Build the NDR recovery sequence to start the same day a courier logs a failed
   delivery.
6. Confirm every message type has an approved WhatsApp Business template before
   the flow can go live.

## Checks
Every figure scoped to India only. Incentive sizing traces to a real RTO-cost
number. No flow step ships on an unapproved template.

## Output
A WhatsApp commerce program spec covering cart recovery, order updates, COD-to-
prepaid and NDR recovery.

## Example
"RTO costs INR 180 per failed COD order on average. COD-to-prepaid nudge offers
INR 50 off - well inside the INR 180 avoided cost - only on pincodes with RTO rate
over 12%. (US brands use the failed-card dunning flow instead, see
life/churn-risk-score.)"

# Lifecycle test program governance

## Purpose
Keeps lifecycle experimentation trustworthy: no confounded tests, one variable at a
time, and a metric and read window fixed before anyone sees a result.

## Steps
1. Check the backlog against currently running tests for any segment-and-metric
   overlap that would confound a read.
2. Rank remaining candidates by expected impact and dependency order (a test whose
   prerequisite is unmet ranks below that prerequisite).
3. Write the hypothesis, control, variant, and minimum sample size for each test.
4. Pre-register the exact metric and read window before launch.
5. Set a holdout, sized in code, for any incrementality read.

## Checks
No two live tests confound each other. Metric and window are fixed before launch,
never chosen after seeing early results.

## Output
A test specification per prioritised test, ready to hand to the workflow that will
build the variant.

## Example
"Win-back discount-timing test queued behind the win-back trigger-timing test
(prerequisite): read discount timing only once trigger timing is settled."

# Monthly lifecycle health review

## Purpose
Reads the full metric chain, tells a volume problem apart from a content problem,
and turns diagnosis into named next actions rather than a status list.

## Steps
1. Pull list growth, opt-in rate, flow and campaign revenue share, deliverability
   and repeat-rate figures for the month from the metric contract.
2. For any weak flow, check whether low entry volume (a segmentation/traffic issue)
   explains it before diagnosing the flow's own content or timing.
3. Pull this month's registry reads; list pending reads as pending, not results.
4. Diagnose the top 2-3 problems with the specific evidence behind each.
5. Recommend the next workflow to run for each diagnosed problem.

## Checks
Volume problems never mis-diagnosed as content problems. No number replaced by an
adjective. Every recommendation names an executing workflow id.

## Output
A monthly report: metric chain, diagnoses with evidence, ranked next actions.

## Example
"Post-purchase flow revenue down 18%: entry volume down 20% (orders down, not the
flow) - fix is order volume, not flow content. No flow change recommended."

# Churn and lapse risk scoring

## Purpose
Builds a churn-risk score from real decay against the customer's own cadence, not a
flat day count, and routes each risk tier to the save program that actually fits
the cause: ordinary win-back, a trust-rebuild win-back for a delivery failure
(return-to-sender for US carriers, RTO for India), or subscription cancel-flow save.

## Steps
1. Compute each customer's expected next-order date from their own purchase
   interval; flag anyone past it by a set margin.
2. Pull subscription pause and failed-renewal events, and set the dunning retry
   schedule for a failed card charge by default; for a failed UPI AutoPay or
   e-mandate renewal (India), set the retry/re-auth schedule per current RBI rules.
3. Pull unresolved support tickets and engagement decay for the same customers.
4. Compute a low/medium/high risk tier per customer in code from the combined
   signals.
5. Route: engagement-decay risk to the ordinary win-back flow; a delivery-failure-
   caused lapse (return-to-sender, or RTO for India) to the trust-rebuild variant;
   active-subscriber risk to the cancel-flow save offer.
6. Report involuntary churn (failed renewals) apart from voluntary cancellations.

## Checks
Order gap always measured against the customer's own cadence. All scoring in code.
A delivery-failure-caused lapse (return-to-sender for US carriers, RTO for India) never routed to a discount-led win-back first.

## Output
A risk-tiered customer list with the routing decision and its evidence.

## Example
"Customer's avg gap: 35 days. Last order: 70 days ago (high risk). Last delivery
failed (return-to-sender) -> route to trust-rebuild win-back, not the standard
discount flow. (India: an RTO event routes the same way.)"

# Post-purchase journey and touchpoint mapping

## Purpose
Maps every touchpoint from order to delivered-and-used, classifies each by the
Kano model, finds the negative peak with real evidence, and designs the delivery
communication and unboxing reveal as the peak worth funding.

## Steps
1. List every real touchpoint (confirmation, shipping update, delivery, unboxing,
   first use, review request).
2. Classify each as basic, performance, or delight, with reasoning.
3. Find the negative peak by reading support tickets and reviews for quoted
   evidence, not assumption.
4. Design the order-status/delivery message set and tracking page aimed at
   keeping WISMO tickets under 5 percent of orders.
5. Design the unboxing reveal and insert tiering as the main peak to fund, capped
   to 2-5 percent of product cost.
6. Name at least one concrete change per touchpoint mapped.

## Checks
Negative peak is evidenced by quotes. Delivery-estimate language never outruns
courier data. Packaging spend stays inside the cost cap.

## Output
A journey map with Kano classes, a delivery communication set, and/or a packaging
brief with its cost model.

## Example
"Negative peak: 'no idea when it's arriving' (14 tickets quoted). Fix: add a
branded tracking page with a live estimate, cutting WISMO by an estimated third."

# Returns and refund flow design

## Purpose
Designs return speed targets, the refund-vs-credit choice, the self-service portal
rules, and failed-delivery/fraud controls (return-to-sender risk for the US;
COD RTO/fraud controls for India), then writes the customer-facing policy text,
checked against law per market.

## Steps
1. Read the live policy and the last quarter's return rate, reasons and refund-
   cycle time from order/support data.
2. Check the legal minimum return window and disclosure per market.
3. Set separate speed targets for time-to-pickup and time-to-refund-after-receipt.
4. Design the refund-vs-credit choice, sizing any credit bonus against real margin.
5. Set self-service rules: what a customer can do alone versus what routes to a
   human (fraud-flagged and high-value returns always route to a human).
6. Set the address-risk/fraud check before a replacement ships (ZIP/address-
   validation history for the US; pincode-level RTO/fraud check for COD orders in
   India).
7. Write the policy text and check it is visible pre-purchase, not just at checkout.
8. Confirm the investment is justified by returners' actual repeat-purchase rate.

## Checks
Policy checked against law per market. Fraud-flagged returns never fully self-
service. Investment level matches the measured repeat-rate lift.

## Output
A returns flow spec plus policy draft text, both dated and market-checked.

## Example
"Time-to-refund target: 3 days after receipt (was 9). Return-to-sender check:
addresses with repeat delivery failures require address confirmation before a
replacement ships. India: pincodes with RTO rate over 15% require ID confirmation
before a COD replacement ships."

# Support reply and ticket-tagging design

## Purpose
Groups real ticket volume into contact types, writes a policy-accurate template
per type, and decides which types are safe to auto-send versus draft-only,
keeping human voice for recovery and VIP moments.

## Steps
1. Read a sample of recent tickets and group into contact types (WISMO, return,
   sizing, damaged/defective, payment, cancel/change, product question,
   complaint), keeping any "other" bucket under 15 percent of volume.
2. Draft a template per type in the brand's voice, citing current policy for every
   factual claim.
3. Classify each type as agent-can-close, agent-can-draft-only, or human-only.
   Recovery and VIP-flagged tickets are never agent-can-close.
4. Write the tagging rule so each incoming ticket maps to exactly one primary tag
   and routes to the right queue and priority.

## Checks
Every claim traces to current policy. Recovery/VIP tickets stay human. No
oversized "other" bucket hiding an uncovered contact type.

## Output
A reply template library plus tagging/routing rules.

## Example
"WISMO template cites the current 5-7 day delivery estimate; agent-can-close if the
order's tracking shows movement, human-only if tracking has been stalled 3+ days."

# AI support agent operating-procedure governance

## Purpose
Writes the exact rules an AI support agent may act on for money-moving actions
(refund cap, order-state limits, who approves above the cap), sets escalation
triggers and identity checks, and proves the ruleset works against real tickets
before go-live, and again after every policy change.

## Steps
1. For every agent-can-close contact type touching money or an account change,
   write the hard cap, the approval path above it, and which order states allow
   the action at all.
2. Set the identity-verification step required before any account or payment
   change.
3. Set escalation triggers: negative sentiment, repeated back-and-forth, an
   explicit request for a human, or ticket value above a threshold, with a warm
   hand-off carrying full conversation history.
4. Replay the drafted ruleset against a sample of last quarter's real tickets,
   scoring accuracy and tone before anything goes live.
5. Set a one-step kill switch and rollback plan for if the agent starts producing
   wrong answers.
6. Re-run the replay after every policy or price change; a stale rulebook is how
   an agent promises something the brand no longer offers.

## Checks
Every money-moving rule has a hard cap and an approval path. Replay uses real
tickets. Escalation always carries full history, never a cold restart.

## Output
An operating-procedure document, a replay test report with scores, and an
escalation rule set.

## Example
"Refund cap: $50 auto-approved if order is delivered and within the return
window; above that, drafts for a human. Replay against 200 past tickets: 94%
correct action, 3 tone flags fixed before go-live."

# Review collection, response and syndication

## Purpose
Times and words review requests around delivery, drafts honest responses
(including to negative reviews), checks which destinations may be incentivised,
and pushes the strongest existing reviews and UGC into the feed, ads and
marketplace listings without ever rewriting them.

## Steps
1. Set request timing about 3 days post-delivery, or defer to the reviews app's
   own optimisation if it already exists.
2. Draft honest, non-pushy request copy.
3. Check which destinations in this request may be incentivised with loyalty
   points (own site: usually yes; Google, most marketplaces: no) and word the
   ask accordingly.
4. Draft an honest, unfiltered response to each new review, especially negative
   ones; flag any review revealing a real defect back to the brand record.
5. Rank reviews and UGC by usefulness (photo attached, specific detail, recency),
   not star rating alone.
6. Select feed rating fields and pull top quotes as ad-copy candidates, noting
   the permission basis, and push allowed content to marketplace listings.

## Checks
No incentive wording where a destination forbids it. No manufactured-sounding
response. Reviews selected and quoted, never rewritten.

## Output
Request copy and timing, draft responses, a defect-flag list, feed-ready fields,
and a review-quote bank for ad copy.

## Example
"Request sent day 3 post-delivery, no points offer since it CCs Google reviews.
Top quote selected for feed: '...true to the photos, fits true to size' (5-star,
photo attached, day 4)."

# Voice-of-customer and CX governance

## Purpose
Starts every VoC cycle from data the brand already owns, clusters open text into
named themes with quotes, keeps a standing NPS/CSAT read, and scores whether the
brand's CX approach is random, intentional or differentiated, with evidence.

## Steps
1. Pool open-text answers from closed support tickets and reviews for the period
   before writing a single new survey question.
2. Cluster the pooled text into named recurring themes with example quotes and a
   count, flagging anything new or growing this period.
3. Run or refresh the standing NPS/CSAT survey, keeping wording unchanged from
   the prior period unless a specific reason is logged.
4. Add a short, attributed staff-input summary.
5. Score CX maturity (random, intentional, differentiated) against a written
   standard, citing specific evidence.
6. Check any new customer-facing tool launched this period against the standard.
7. Route confirmed recurring themes to the specialist workflow that owns the fix.

## Checks
Owned data reviewed before surveying. Every theme has a quoted example. Every new
tool checked, none launched unchecked.

## Output
A theme-clustered report, an NPS/CSAT trend, and a CX maturity score with evidence.

## Example
"Theme: 'sizing runs small' - 22 mentions this quarter, up from 9 last quarter.
Routed to Product specialist and to the PDP copy. CX maturity: intentional (a
written standard exists and is checked), not yet differentiated."

# Offer package design from margin and AOV

## Purpose
Builds a full offer package, price, bundle, gift, guarantee and upsell placement,
around the buyer's single biggest objection and the brand's real margin and order-
value distribution, not the average AOV or a copied competitor structure.

## Steps
1. Pull landed cost per SKU and the real order-value distribution (not just the
   average), plus the buyer's stated biggest objection from the brand record.
2. Write the value proposition to answer that specific objection, scored against
   the value equation (dream outcome, likelihood, time, effort).
3. Build the SKU margin waterfall and contribution per order in code.
4. Map the product's use journey into bundle/quantity-ladder tiers, sizing each to
   clear the contribution floor, with a justified reason per tier and a pre-
   selected middle option.
5. Design any gift-with-purchase to help use the core product, sized to lift the
   target tier, never dishonestly framed.
6. Place upsell/cross-sell offers by friction level (cart, checkout, post-
   purchase), anchored high with a cheaper down-sell.
7. Cost the guarantee from real refund data and write it in if-not-X-in-Y-we-will-Z
   form, activated at delivery.
8. Run the whole package through life/discount-policy-check and set the test plan
   (metric, read window) before it launches.

## Checks
Every tier clears the contribution floor. Guarantee cost is real, not assumed. No
revenue-only or ROAS-only justification accepted for go/no-go.

## Output
{package: {price, terms, bundle, gift, guarantee}, objection_answered,
margin_waterfall_ref, contribution_per_order, discount_policy_check, test_plan}

## Example
"3-pack ladder at $18/24/30 (per-unit price steps down each tier), middle
pre-selected; GWP: travel pouch on the 3-pack only; guarantee: 'not a perfect fit
in 30 days, free exchange'; contribution/order still clears $7 floor on every tier."

# Discount policy and price-integrity check

## Purpose
The single gate every discount, bundle, GWP or campaign-discount decision passes
through, so discounting never quietly trains buyers to wait and never crosses a
founder's stated line.

## Steps
1. Check the proposed discount's frequency against the standing cap for this
   segment and period.
2. Check conditionality: does it require a real condition (minimum order, first-
   time, loyalty tier) rather than a blanket cut.
3. Check framing: is any reference price a real prior selling price, is any
   urgency claim real.
4. Check against every founder red line on record.
5. If a rule is unclear or a red line is missing for this case, fail the check
   and ask the founder rather than guessing.

## Checks
Fails closed on ambiguity. Every failure names the exact rule broken.

## Output
{pass_or_fail, rule_cited, fix_if_failed}

## Example
"FAIL: monthly frequency cap for this segment already used (2 of 2 in policy).
Rule: 'no segment sees more than 2 discount sends per month' (policy v3)."

# Subscription offer and cancel-flow design

## Purpose
Makes the reason to subscribe stronger than a flat discount, and designs a cancel
flow that is as easy to complete as sign-up but tries a reason-matched
alternative and a costed save offer before the subscriber leaves.

## Steps
1. Compare the subscription's total value (price, perks, flexibility) against the
   plain discount it replaces, in real numbers.
2. Set cadence flexibility and perk gating tied to actual use, not an arbitrary
   spend line.
3. Build the cancel flow as four stages: benefit reminder, exit-reason survey, a
   reason-matched alternative (pause, swap, frequency change), then a conditional,
   costed save offer only if earlier stages fail.
4. Cost the save offer against the subscriber's own order count and value.
5. Cap pause/skip/delay abuse without breaking a genuine flexibility need.
6. Add non-monetary mechanics (streaks, milestone gifts) as an addition, tested
   against a discount-only save, not assumed superior.
7. Set per-stage save-rate tracking so a weak stage can be rewritten specifically.

## Checks
Cancel is as easy to complete as sign-up. Save offer sized in code to the
subscriber's own value. Non-monetary mechanic tested, not assumed.

## Output
A subscription offer spec and a four-stage cancel-flow design with per-stage
save-rate targets.

## Example
"Stage 3 (reason: 'too much product') offers a frequency change to every 8 weeks,
not a discount; only subscribers who still exit reach stage 4's 15% save offer."

# Referral, partner and payment-term offer design

## Purpose
Sizes a referral reward and partner perk from real margin and repeat-buyer value,
and designs installment/BNPL and trial pricing with the real provider fee shown,
never a copied structure from a competitor.

## Steps
1. Size the give-X-get-X reward from the repeat-buyer base's real average value.
2. Set the tracking mechanism (code or link) and the reward-payout trigger, which
   fires only on a confirmed, non-refunded order.
3. Identify partner brands serving the same customer without competing on
   category, for a no-cost cross-promotion perk.
4. Design installment/BNPL terms with the real per-installment price and the
   payment provider's real fee shown against margin.
5. Design a nominal-price trial with a disclosed conversion date and full price.
6. Clear both the referral reward and the trial/BNPL terms through
   life/discount-policy-check.

## Checks
Reward and any bonus sized to real margin. Payment-provider fees are real, not
estimated. Trial conversion terms disclosed to the buyer up front.

## Output
A referral offer spec, a partner candidate list, and a BNPL/trial pricing spec.

## Example
"Give $10, get $10, capped at 1 reward per order pair, paid only after the
referred order ships without a return - protects margin against return abuse."

# Offer test sequencing

## Purpose
Keeps offer testing honest: structure tested before depth, one variable at a time,
with the metric and read window fixed before launch and no duplicate tests
running for the same underlying question.

## Steps
1. Pull every proposed offer/bundle/GWP/upsell/guarantee test not yet run.
2. Sequence so a structural question (does a bundle beat a single SKU) is tested
   before a depth question (which bundle size wins).
3. Check dependency order: a test needing a working discount-policy rule ranks
   below getting that rule settled.
4. Pre-register the exact metric and read window for each test before launch.
5. Remove duplicate or already-run tests from the backlog.

## Checks
No test changes two variables at once. No dependent test runs ahead of its
prerequisite. No duplicate test for the same offer question.

## Output
A sequenced, dependency-checked backlog, each entry pre-registered.

## Example
"Bundle-vs-single-SKU (structure) sequenced ahead of 3-pack-vs-5-pack (depth) for
the same product, since depth only matters if structure already won."

# Gift card program design

## Purpose
Designs the gift card as a real product line, denominations, expiry, bulk-gifting
terms, and its interaction with refund credit, while modelling the unredeemed-
balance liability so the founder sees the cash-flow effect before launch.

## Steps
1. Read current denominations and redemption rate if a gift-card app exists.
2. Choose sellable denominations and any bonus-value tier, sized against margin.
3. Set expiry policy checked against each market's legal minimum validity.
4. Design a separate bulk/corporate-gifting tier and process.
5. Set the rule for how a refund-issued store credit interacts with a purchased
   gift card, so a refund credit is never expired like a promotional one.
6. Model the float liability (unredeemed balance) in code from stated sell-through
   assumptions.
7. Write the purchase-confirmation, pre-expiry-reminder and redemption-receipt
   copy.

## Checks
Expiry never conflicts with legal minimums. Float liability computed in code.
Refund credit and purchased gift card follow different expiry rules.

## Output
A gift-card program design, a float-liability model, and the reminder flow copy.

## Example
"$25/50/100 denominations, no bonus tier at launch. Float liability at
6-month sell-through assumption: $4,200 outstanding balance modeled."

# Proactive outreach: chat, phone and voice/IVR

## Purpose
Designs the three outbound-initiated concierge channels, proactive chat for a
high-intent visitor, a phone queue for high-AOV abandoners, and automated IVR for
order-confirmation (dunning follow-up for a failed card by default, COD confirmation
for India) and satisfaction checks, each with its own trigger and channel fit, never
dialling or sending on its own.

## Steps
1. Define the intent signals that qualify a visitor for proactive chat (visit
   count, product viewed, known VIP status).
2. Write a specific opener per signal, never a generic greeting, with a cap on
   how often one visitor is approached.
3. Set the AOV or product-category threshold above which a phone call beats
   email/SMS, from the brand's own AOV distribution.
4. Write call scripts per scenario (cart-abandon, pre-purchase question, VIP
   check-in) and build the ranked daily call queue by value and recency.
5. Choose which events justify automated IVR (order pre-dispatch confirmation,
   delivery-failure follow-up, post-resolution satisfaction check; COD pre-dispatch
   confirmation for India) and write the IVR scripts, matching the quiet-hour rules
   already set for SMS/WhatsApp.
6. Set outcome logging for chat, call and IVR back into the customer record.

## Checks
Every signal and threshold is specific and evidence-based. IVR quiet hours match
the standing channel policy. A human places every call; nothing auto-dials.

## Output
A proactive-chat opener set, a ranked call queue with scripts, and IVR scripts
with cadence.

## Example
"AOV threshold: $500 (top decile of orders). Cart-abandon script for this tier
opens: 'Saw you were looking at the sapphire set - happy to answer sizing
questions before you decide.'"

# Marketplace seller-support queue management

## Purpose
Runs marketplace buyer-seller messages and guarantee claims on each marketplace's
own response clock (about 48 hours for a message, about 72 for a claim), kept
separate from the brand's own helpdesk SLAs and tagging.

## Steps
1. Pull the open queue from each marketplace's own seller console and tag every
   item with its own deadline.
2. Draft the buyer-message response inside that window, in the brand's voice.
3. Assemble the delivery proof and correspondence log a claim needs, matched to
   what that specific marketplace accepts as evidence.
4. Draft the claim response with that evidence, inside the claim's own clock.
5. Track claim rate and reason over time, flagging a rising rate to the
   returns/fulfilment specialist.

## Checks
Every response respects its own marketplace's clock; missing the message-window
deadline can itself trigger a claim right. Queue and SLA tracking stay separate
from the brand's own helpdesk.

## Output
Drafted responses inside each clock, plus a claim-rate trend report.

## Example
"Buyer message at hour 40 of the 48-hour Amazon window: drafted and flagged
urgent. Claim rate this month: 0.4% of orders, flat versus last month. (India:
same process on Flipkart/Myntra's own clock.)"

# Mystery-shopper journey audit (CX leg)

## Purpose
Walks the brand's own post-purchase and support experience as a real customer
would and catalogues every place it falls short of what the brand itself states,
with evidence, then routes each gap to the specialist who owns the fix.

## Steps
1. Place a real or test-gateway order, logging every step's timestamp.
2. Quote every promise made at checkout and in the confirmation (delivery
   estimate, guarantee terms) verbatim.
3. Send a genuine, realistic support question through the brand's own channel.
4. Time the actual response against what the brand states or implies as its
   response time.
5. Catalogue every gap between promise and reality, each with a timestamp,
   screenshot or quoted message as evidence.
6. Route each gap to the owning workflow (delivery communication, support
   templates, checkout).

## Checks
Every gap is evidenced, not impressionistic. Comparison uses the brand's own
stated promise, never an assumed industry standard.

## Output
A gap catalogue, each entry routed to a named owning workflow or agent.

## Example
"Promise: '2-4 day delivery.' Reality: delivered day 6, no proactive update sent.
Routed to LIFE-W13 (delivery communication) for a stronger mid-transit update."

# Corporate gifting sales desk

## Purpose
Runs B2B gifting orders end to end: qualifying the enquiry or building the
outbound list in season, quoting from the standing bulk tiers, preparing a
sales-tax-correct invoice (GST-correct for India), planning delivery to many
addresses, and setting up next season's repeat-order reminder.

## Steps
1. Qualify an inbound enquiry for quantity, budget and occasion, or build the
   outbound lead list starting 90 days before the target Q4 holiday season
   (or festival, for India).
2. Quote using the standing bulk pricing tiers, checked against margin; anything
   beyond the standing tiers is founder_gate.
3. Confirm custom packaging or engraving options and their real lead time.
4. Prepare a sales-tax invoice, checked against state nexus and resale-
   certificate rules; for India, prepare a GST-compliant invoice checked against
   the current rate and the buyer's GSTIN if given.
5. Plan delivery to each recipient address, checking courier serviceability for
   every one before the order is confirmed.
6. Set a repeat-order reminder for next season, timed to the same lead-time rule.

## Checks
Quote stays inside the standing bulk tiers, or is gated. Sales-tax (or GST, for
India) invoice checked against the current rule with date. Every address checked
for serviceability.

## Output
A bulk quote, a sales-tax invoice draft (a GST invoice draft for India), a
split-delivery plan, and a repeat-order reminder.

## Example
"50-unit corporate order, standard bulk tier 3 ($38/unit). Engraving lead time:
5 business days, confirmed against the partner's stated capacity. (India: same
process, quoted in INR with a GST invoice.)"

# Consumer-complaint and compliance notice queue

## Purpose
Runs the consumer-complaint and regulatory-notice queue: BBB complaints, state
consumer-complaint portal cases and FTC referrals by default, each on that
channel's own SLA; India only, the statutory grievance queue India's E-Commerce
Rules require instead, every grievance acknowledged in 48 hours and resolved in
1 month. Consumer-forum and legal notices are tracked on their own separate,
stricter clock in both cases.

## Steps
1. Log every complaint the moment it arrives, starting its clock from actual
   receipt.
2. Send the acknowledgement inside the receiving channel's SLA (about 2 weeks for
   BBB/state portals; within 48 hours for India's statutory rule).
3. Investigate against the order/policy record and prepare the resolution inside
   the channel's own window (1-month statutory window for India).
4. Track any BBB case, state consumer-complaint case or legal notice (an
   e-Daakhil consumer-forum case for India) on its own separate clock and status,
   never merged into the ordinary complaint SLA.
5. Run the weekly check across every open item, showing days remaining or days
   breached, in code.
6. Escalate anything nearing or past deadline to the founder immediately, not at
   the next weekly cycle.
7. Log the resolution and closure date against the applicable deadline.

## Checks
Both India statutory windows tracked in code where they apply; BBB/state SLA
tracked in code for the US. Legal notices never merged into the ordinary queue.
Nothing nearing breach left unescalated.

## Output
A logged queue with SLA clocks, an acknowledgement record, resolution drafts, and
a weekly SLA compliance report.

## Example
"Complaint logged Tuesday 3pm. Acknowledged Thursday 1pm. India: within the
48-hour statutory window; resolution due within 30 days, flagged for escalation
at day 25 if still open. US: within the BBB/state portal's own target window."

# Warranty, repair and after-sales service queue

## Purpose
Runs resizing, repair, re-plating, warranty and buyback/exchange requests end to
end: intake, coverage determination, courier pickup, repair-partner routing,
status updates, and cost-per-case tracking against the warranty reserve.

## Steps
1. Log the request type, product and purchase date.
2. Check the purchase date against the warranty window and determine coverage
   (in-warranty, paid out-of-warranty, or buyback/exchange), citing the specific
   clause.
3. Book courier pickup, confirming address and item with the customer first.
4. Route the item to the correct repair partner with a turnaround matched to
   that partner's real stated capacity.
5. Send a status update at intake, at drop-off, and at return dispatch, each
   reflecting a real status change.
6. Track the case's real cost (courier both ways, partner fee, any part) in code
   against the warranty reserve.
7. Close the case once the customer confirms receipt or the exchange completes.

## Checks
Coverage determination cites the specific warranty clause. Turnaround matches the
partner's real capacity. Cost computed in code from real invoices.

## Output
Logged and routed requests, status updates, per-case cost tracking, and closed
case records.

## Example
"Resizing request, purchased 4 months ago (in-warranty). Pickup booked, routed to
in-house jeweller, 3-day turnaround. Cost: $0 to customer, $18 to the reserve."

# Branded customer community design

## Purpose
Checks whether a peer-to-peer, always-on community actually fits the brand's
repeat-buyer base before building one, then designs the structure, moderation and
a light engagement calendar distinct from the campaign calendar and the support
inbox.

## Steps
1. Check the brand's repeat, high-engagement buyer count and engagement level
   against what sustains a community; recommend go or no-go with the evidence.
2. Choose the platform (Slack, Discord, Circle) and design the channel structure
   around named use cases (product help, early access, feedback).
3. Write the moderation policy, especially how a public complaint routes to the
   real support queue instead of being handled in public.
4. Build a light, sustainable engagement calendar (prompts, early-access drops,
   AMAs), distinct from the weekly campaign calendar.
5. Set when a founder or team member should show up in person versus stay quiet.
6. Set the path for a recurring community theme to reach the VoC record.
7. Track membership, active-member share, and the repeat-purchase rate of
   members versus non-members, in code.

## Checks
Go/no-go is grounded in real evidence, not enthusiasm. Complaints always route to
support. Member-vs-non-member comparison computed in code.

## Output
A community structure and moderation policy, an engagement calendar, and a
recurring health note.

## Example
"1,400 repeat buyers, 30% opened last 3 emails - enough base to test. Discord,
3 channels (help, early-access, feedback). Members' repeat-purchase rate tracked
against a matched non-member cohort from launch."

# Organic channel and platform strategy

## Purpose
Decide which platforms a brand organically runs, with a reason tied to the avatar and a fixed test window for anything new, not a copy of what competitors do.

## Steps
1. Read the avatar, category, region and voice from the brand brain, including whether Spanish or another language outperforms English captions for this audience, and the mobile-only browsing share. India only (markets IN, reads null for a US-only brand): note whether the avatar buys on WhatsApp, and whether Hindi or a regional language outperforms English captions.
2. Pull the competitive teardown for structure and cadence only, never text or footage.
3. Score each platform: avatar fit, cost to produce one week of content, a 2-week trial success bar.
4. Set 3-5 content pillars, each naming a SKU and the objection it answers.
5. Lock the visual world (palette, type, caption style) so every account reads as one brand.
6. Write the account setup checklist and a platform-policy compliance check.
7. Package as a plain-English card for the founder to approve any new account, platform drop, or account-type change.

## Checks
- Every pillar names a SKU and an objection.
- No platform runs past its trial date without a founder decision.
- Visual spec matches approved brand assets.

## Output
{positioning_brief, platform_plan[], visual_world_spec, account_setup_checklist}

## Example
Pillar "Why it does not wobble on potholed US streets" ties to the SKU "stroller-v2" and the objection "will it survive potholes", scheduled 2x a week on Instagram and YouTube Shorts only, with Pinterest on a 2-week trial ending 15 Oct.

# Buyer and avatar question mapping

## Purpose
One shared source of real buyer language feeds both the content calendar (org/make-content) and the SEO page-brief pipeline (org/page-brief-build), so scripts and pages answer the same questions buyers actually ask, not guessed ones.

## Steps
1. Pull 90 days of support tickets, comments and DMs tagged with a product question.
2. Pull review text from Amazon, Walmart, Google and the site for the same SKUs (also Flipkart, India market option, reads null for a US-only brand). Quote the exact line and note the source and date.
3. Pull Search Console queries where connected; label People Also Ask and autocomplete pulls as web research, kept apart from private data.
4. Cluster by SKU and funnel stage: awareness objection, decision-stage spec question, post-purchase how-to.
5. Tag each cluster with a suggested channel: an objection with strong emotion or visual proof suits short video; a spec or comparison question suits a page; a trust or authority question suits the facts page.
6. Rank by how often the question appears and how close it sits to a stuck SKU.

## Checks
- Every question carries a quoted source and a date.
- No invented question.
- Each cluster names a real SKU.

## Output
{questions[{text, sku, funnel_stage, suggested_channel, sources[], count}]}

## Example
"Will the folding hinge rust after a rainy Seattle winter?" - stroller-v2, decision-stage, suggested_channel: page + video, 14 mentions across reviews and DMs since June.

# Make organic content (dispatcher)

## Purpose
Route a content task to the one child skill built for its format, instead of one generic writer trying to do video, carousel, long-form, Pinterest and email equally well. This is the parent node of the make-content family; it holds no drafting logic itself.

## Steps
1. Read the task's format and platform fields.
2. Match to exactly one child: org/make-content/short-video, /carousel, /youtube-long, /pinterest-pin, or /newsletter.
3. Pass the named SKU, named buyer, the objection or question the piece answers, brand voice file, claims tiers, and any Scout references straight through unchanged.
4. Take the child's draft and run shared/claim-check before returning it to the calling workflow.
5. If the task names a format with no child (a new platform), stop and hand a workflow proposal to a person instead of guessing a format.

- Exactly one child skill is invoked per task.
- No draft returns without a claims-check verdict attached.
- A format with no matching child stops the run rather than improvising.

## Output
Whatever the matched child returns, wrapped with {claims_check_verdict}.

## Example
A calendar slot marked format: "reel", platform: "instagram" routes to org/make-content/short-video; a slot marked format: "pin" routes to org/make-content/pinterest-pin.

# Short-video script and shot list

## Purpose
Turn one SKU and one buyer into a script a camera-phone crew can film without asking a follow-up question, sized for 15-45 seconds.

## Steps
1. Name the one reaction, action or takeaway the video proves in its first 3 seconds.
2. Write the hook: 5-8 words, must work with sound off, appears on screen inside the first second.
3. Write the body cutting jargon and repeated synonyms; one claim per line, each checked against the claims tiers.
4. Write a caption addressed to one named buyer (never "you guys"), then the CTA and where it points.
5. Build a shot list: shot number, framing (close/mid/wide), location, which SKU or prop, on-screen text, seconds per shot, totalling the target run time.
6. Flag anything blocking a film day: founder availability, a location not yet scouted, a prop out of stock.

## Checks
- Hook works muted.
- Every factual line traces to a claims tier.
- Shot list seconds sum to the target length.
- Below tenth-grade reading level.

## Output
{hook, body, caption, cta, claims_used[], shot_list[], flags[]}

## Example
Hook: "This stroller survived my building's broken lift." Shot 1: mid shot, lobby, stroller-v2, on-screen text "Day 40", 3s.

# Carousel script and slide list

## Purpose
Give design a slide-by-slide brief for one argument (a comparison, a myth-bust, a how-to), sized to finish in 5-9 slides so swipe-through does not drop off.

## Steps
1. Pick the single argument the carousel makes. One carousel, one point.
2. Write slide 1: the hook, readable in under 2 seconds, stating the stakes.
3. Write slides 2 through 7-9: one idea per slide, short lines, one heading plus one supporting line each.
4. Write the closing slide: a one-line recap and one CTA.
5. Write the caption for readers who read captions before swiping; apply the same claims tiers.
6. List every slide's heading, supporting text and image direction for the designer.

## Checks
- One idea per slide, no slide carrying two arguments.
- Every factual line is claims-tier checked.
- Total slides between 5 and 9.

## Output
{hook_slide, slides[], closing_slide, caption, cta, claims_used[]}

## Example
Argument: "Why our hinge outlasts the $40 stroller." Slide 3 heading: "200,000 fold cycles tested", supporting: "our lab number, dated March 2026".

# YouTube long-form script and structure

## Purpose
Long-form succeeds or fails on retention curve, not hook alone; this skill forces a payoff-first open and a chapter structure that survives the edit, distinct from a short-video hook script.

## Steps
1. Pick the single search or watch intent the video serves, sourced from org/buyer-question-mapping (a how-to, a comparison, a founder story).
2. Write the first 15 seconds stating exactly what the viewer gets and why the runtime is worth it.
3. Outline 3-6 chapters with a timestamp label each.
4. Write the script per chapter, one claim per line, tier-checked.
5. Write the title (keyword-forward, under 60 characters) and description, keyword in the first two lines, links after.
6. Suggest tags and an end-screen plan (subscribe, next video, or a site link).

## Checks
- The payoff is stated in the first 15 seconds.
- Chapters cover the whole runtime without a gap.
- Title and first description line both carry the target keyword.

## Output
{title, description, chapters[], script_by_chapter[], tags[], end_screen_plan, claims_used[]}

Title: "Stroller hinge test: 6 months, 3 US cities" - chapter 2 "0:45 The pothole test" with its own script block and one tiered claim.
