# Model Amazon channel economics

## Purpose
Amazon's referral fee, FBA fee and storage cost stack up in ways that are easy to underestimate from memory. This
skill models the full stack in code against a SKU's real landed cost, so a launch or continuation decision is made
on a real net margin, not a gross-margin illusion.

## Steps
1. Pull the current, dated Amazon fee stack for the category: referral fee percentage, FBA pick-pack-ship fee by
   size tier, and storage cost by month.
2. Model the full fee stack against the SKU's landed cost, computed in code, never estimated.
3. Add a stated PPC budget assumption (clearly labeled as an assumption) and the storage cost for the SKU's actual
   size tier.
4. Check the resulting Amazon price against the brand's DTC price-parity rule, using the current live DTC price,
   not a stale one.
5. Compute net margin after every fee line, in code, and flag any SKU whose net margin falls below the brand's own
   stated floor.

## Checks
- Every fee line is sourced from Amazon's currently published rate card, dated.
- Net margin is computed in code, never estimated in prose.
- Price parity is checked against the live DTC price at the time of the check.

## Output
{fee_stack, net_margin_per_sku[], parity_check, margin_floor_flags[]}

## Example
SKU-1042: referral fee 15%, FBA fee $3.50 (size tier standard), storage $0.15/unit/month. Landed cost $8.50, Amazon
price $24.99. Net margin after all fees and a $1.50 PPC assumption: 19%, above the brand's 15% floor. Parity check:
Amazon price matches DTC within the allowed band.

# Build a marketplace listing

## Purpose
Every marketplace enforces its own title length, bullet rules, image slots and attribute set, and none of them are
the same. This is the parent procedure: it never posts a listing itself, only drafts one, and it always routes to
the platform-specific child before writing a single field. Amazon, Walmart, Target Plus, eBay and TikTok Shop are
the default US-first children; Flipkart/Myntra/Nykaa and Blinkit/Zepto are grouped India-market options (markets:
IN), not selected for a US-only brand.

## Steps
1. Confirm the target marketplace and select the matching child skill
   (`prod/list-on-marketplace/amazon`, `/walmart`, `/target-plus`, `/ebay`, `/tiktok-shop`, or, for an India brand,
   `/flipkart-myntra-nykaa` or `/blinkit-zepto`).
2. Run the child's specific field rules to place the top keyword and write benefit-led, claim-checked copy in the
   platform's own format.
3. Brief every image slot to that platform's own size, crop and content rule: an Amazon main image and a
   TikTok Shop video cover are not interchangeable.
4. Fill every attribute field the platform requires and confirm the correct category node in that platform's own
   taxonomy.
5. Package the finished draft for a named human to paste into the seller console. This skill never posts directly
   to a live listing on any platform.

## Checks
- The marketplace named is one of the seven supported children, matched to its own child procedure.
- No required field is left blank.
- Nothing produced by this skill is ever posted directly; it is always handed to a human.

## Output
{marketplace, listing_draft, image_briefs[], attributes{}, category_node}

## Example
Marketplace: target-plus. Routed to `prod/list-on-marketplace/target-plus`. Title and key callouts placed per
Target's own style guide; 5 image slots briefed to Target's spec; attributes filled; draft handed to the
marketplace manager to paste into Target Plus's Partners Online portal. India: the equivalent nykaa listing routes
to `prod/list-on-marketplace/flipkart-myntra-nykaa` instead (markets: IN).

# List on Amazon

## Purpose
Amazon ranks primarily on the title and backend keywords, and converts primarily on the bullets and images. This
skill writes to that structure specifically, not a generic product-page template.

## Steps
1. Place the single highest-priority keyword in the title, positioned where Amazon's search weighs it most, and
   repeat it in the first bullet.
2. Write 5 benefit-led bullets, each carrying exactly one true, tiered claim: never a bullet with two unrelated
   claims stacked together.
3. Brief every image slot Amazon allows (main image on white background, lifestyle, infographic, size/comparison,
   in-use) to Amazon's exact spec for that slot.
4. Fill every backend attribute field completely and set backend search terms with keywords not already used in
   the visible copy, to avoid wasting indexing space.

## Checks
- The top keyword appears in both the title and the first bullet.
- Every bullet's claim is in the approved or site-backed tier, checked before handoff.

## Output
{listing_draft, image_briefs[], attributes{}, backend_keywords[]}

## Example
Title places "leak-proof steel water bottle 1L" with the top keyword first. Bullet 1 repeats it with the leak-proof
claim, cited to the site's own drop-test page. 5 image slots briefed including a size-comparison infographic.
Backend terms add non-duplicate synonyms like "insulated flask."

# List on Walmart Marketplace

## Purpose
Walmart's title style, required GTIN/UPC and Content Hub rich-media rules differ from Amazon's, and its search
ranking (grading via the Listing Quality score) weighs different fields. A copy-pasted Amazon listing under-
performs here.

## Steps
1. Place the top keyword in the title, respecting Walmart's own character limit and title-style guide, which
   discourages promotional language Amazon tolerates.
2. Write the key features and long description in Walmart's own field structure, matching its Listing Quality
   scoring criteria.
3. Brief every image slot Walmart allows to its own spec, including any Content Hub rich-media module the
   category supports.
4. Fill every category-specific attribute Walmart requires and confirm a valid GTIN or UPC is attached; a missing
   or invalid GTIN blocks the listing outright.

## Checks
- The title respects Walmart's character limit and style rule for the specific category.
- A valid GTIN/UPC is present; the listing does not go live without one.

{listing_draft, image_briefs[], attributes{}}

## Example
Category: kitchen. Title kept within Walmart's limit, promotional language removed per its style guide. GTIN
validated against GS1. Attribute "capacity_in_quarts" filled with the exact number, not "large."

# List on eBay

## Purpose
eBay's Best Match ranking weighs Item Specifics, seller performance (Top Rated Seller status), return policy and
handling time as heavily as the listing copy itself, so a listing missing these is invisible in search even with
strong copy.

## Steps
1. Place the top keyword in the title within eBay's character limit, front-loading the most searched term.
2. Fill every Item Specific field the category supports; Best Match rewards completeness here more than on a
   general marketplace.
3. Brief the image slots to eBay's spec: at least 12 images where the category allows, zoomable, no watermarks
   or border text.
4. Set the return policy and handling time explicitly; a shorter handling time and a buyer-friendly return
   policy both lift Best Match ranking and Top Rated Seller eligibility.

## Checks
- Every relevant Item Specific field is filled, none left blank.
- The return policy and handling time are deliberately set, not left at a platform default.

## Output
{listing_draft, image_briefs[], attributes{}, return_policy}

## Example
Category: sporting goods. All 18 available Item Specifics filled. 14 images briefed, zoomable. Return policy set
to 30-day buyer-paid return, handling time set to 1 business day, both chosen to support Top Rated Seller status.

# List on TikTok Shop

## Purpose
TikTok Shop sells primarily through in-feed video and LIVE shopping, not a browsed catalogue page: the listing
exists to be tagged into video and LIVE content and to support the creator affiliate program, so it needs a video
cover and a commission decision a standard catalogue listing does not.

## Steps
1. Write a short, benefit-led title and description built for a video-first shopping surface, not a dense
   marketplace-style bullet list.
2. Brief the product image and short-form video cover to TikTok Shop's spec, since the cover image is what shows
   in-feed before a viewer taps through.
3. Fill every required attribute and confirm the category placement supports in-feed and LIVE product tagging.
4. Set the creator affiliate commission rate and any GMV Max (TikTok's automated ad) settings the brand approves,
   since affiliate reach is a primary driver of sales here, not organic browse.

## Checks
- The listing is tagged for in-feed/LIVE product linking, not left as a standalone catalogue-only page.
- Every claim appearing in a linked video script or caption is approved or site-backed, same as any other channel.

## Output
{listing_draft, video_cover_brief, attributes{}, affiliate_commission}

## Example
Product: a skincare serum. Title short and benefit-led ("Overnight glow serum"). Video cover briefed to show the
product in use in the first second. Affiliate commission set at 15% to attract creator participation.

# List on Flipkart, Myntra and Nykaa

## Purpose
India only (markets: IN): this skill covers the brand's other major India marketplaces beyond Amazon, in one
grouped child since they share the underlying discipline (a platform-specific title/attribute set, none of them
Amazon) while differing on their specialty. It does not run for a US-only brand, whose non-Amazon options are
Walmart, Target Plus, eBay and TikTok Shop instead.

## Steps
1. Confirm which of the three platforms this listing targets: Flipkart (general marketplace), Myntra
   (fashion-specific), or Nykaa (beauty/wellness-specific), since each has its own title length, attribute set
   and search weighting.
2. Place the top keyword in the title, respecting that platform's own character limit, which is often shorter and
   stricter than a general marketplace.
3. On Myntra, confirm a size chart is present and correct for the category before the listing is considered
   complete: its absence is a common cause of size-related returns. On Nykaa, run every beauty or wellness claim
   through the claim-check skill before it goes near the draft; an unsupported claim about skin or health effects
   is a compliance risk, not just a marketing overreach, and is removed rather than softened.
4. Brief every image slot the platform allows to its own spec, including a mandatory size-chart image for Myntra
   apparel or an ingredient-list/texture-shot image for Nykaa beauty listings.
5. Fill every category-specific attribute the platform requires: fabric/fit/occasion for Myntra, skin-type/
   concern/ingredient for Nykaa (matching the real product formulation, never a category-typical guess), or the
   platform's own generic attribute set for Flipkart.

## Checks
- Every Myntra apparel listing has a size chart present before it is considered complete.
- Every Nykaa beauty or wellness claim passed claim-check before the listing is considered complete.
- Category-specific attributes carry real, specific values, never a generic placeholder.

## Output
{marketplace, listing_draft, size_chart, image_briefs[], attributes{}}

## Example
Marketplace: nykaa. Product: a face serum. Claim "reduces the look of fine lines" kept (site-backed by a 4-week
user trial). Claim "clinically proven" removed (no clinical trial exists in the brand record). Ingredient
attribute filled with the exact INCI list.

# List on Blinkit and Zepto

## Purpose
India only (markets: IN): quick commerce listings on Blinkit and Zepto are read at thumbnail size on a phone in
seconds, not read in depth like a marketplace product page; this grouped child covers both since they share the
same thumbnail-first discipline while each keeps its own app layout, category tree and crop rule. It does not run
for a US-only brand, whose rapid-delivery/grocery listings (Instacart, DoorDash, Gopuff) are built under the
quick-commerce-onboard skill instead, since those platforms are not part of this marketplace tree.

## Steps
1. Write a short, scan-friendly title that reads clearly even at small thumbnail size: no long benefit strings,
   just what the product is and its pack size.
2. Confirm the pack size and MRP shown are exact and match the brand's current, live pricing; a stale MRP here is
   a common source of the ROAS-distortion problem these platforms' own dashboards create.
3. Brief the thumbnail image to the chosen platform's own small-format spec, checked for legibility at the actual
   render size in the app, not assumed identical between Blinkit and Zepto: a thumbnail crop that works on one can
   clip the product on the other, so each is built separately even for the same SKU.
4. Confirm the correct dark-store category placement in that platform's own category tree.

## Checks
- The title is legible and clear when previewed at actual thumbnail size.
- The MRP shown matches the current live price exactly.

## Output
{marketplace, listing_draft, thumbnail_brief, category_placement}

## Example
Product: 500ml juice bottle. Title: "Brand Fresh Juice 500ml": reads clearly at thumbnail size. MRP confirmed
against the live price file. Built separately for Blinkit's and Zepto's own crop and category tree rather than
reused as-is.

# Check US labelling and quality-marking compliance (FTC, Care Labeling, Prop 65)

## Purpose
A marketplace can pull a listing, or worse, penalize the account, for a missing FTC precious-metal quality mark, a missing textile Care Labeling Rule disclosure, or a missing Prop 65 warning. This check runs before a listing is built, not after a takedown notice. India: the same job checks BIS hallmarking and Legal Metrology labelling instead (markets: IN, reads null for US brands).

## Steps
1. Identify which compliance requirement applies to this specific category: the FTC Jewelry Guides quality mark (precious-metal jewellery), the Care Labeling Rule (fibre content, origin, care for textiles), a Prop 65 warning, or a CPSC rule (India: BIS certification for hardware/electronics/toys, hallmarking for jewellery, or Legal Metrology labelling; markets: IN).
2. Confirm the current certification, hallmark or disclosure status and its expiry date from the brand's own compliance record, not from an assumption that "it was fine last time."
3. If a required certification or disclosure is missing or expired, block the listing build entirely until it is resolved; do not proceed with a caveat or a "list now, fix later" workaround.

## Checks
- No listing for a regulated category proceeds to build before this check explicitly clears.
- Certification status is read from a recorded, dated fact, never assumed current.

## Output
{category_requirements[], certification_status, cleared}

## Output note
A real-time India BIS/hallmarking registry API was not found in the wave-2 research pass (markets: IN); that variant of this check reads a human-recorded status (BIS Care app or equivalent, checked by a person) rather than verifying a hallmark itself.

## Example
Category: gold jewellery, US listing. FTC Jewelry Guides quality mark (karat stamp, trademark) on file, documentation current. Cleared: true. India: the same jewellery SKU also needs a BIS hallmark certificate on file (markets: IN); a second SKU in the same batch had none, cleared: false, listing build blocked until resolved.

# Prepare an FBA inbound shipment

## Purpose
FBA's dimension and weight limits change, and an outdated cached limit produces a rejected or delayed shipment.
Keeping the full paper trail matters because it is the only evidence available if inventory goes missing in
Amazon's own warehouse.

## Steps
1. Measure the actual case dimensions and check them against FBA's currently published hard limits, pulled fresh
   rather than from a cached figure from a past shipment.
2. Reuse a saved shipment template whenever this SKU and case size match a shipment already sent successfully,
   to avoid re-deriving the plan from scratch each time.
3. Build the shipment plan: box count, weight per box (checked under the carrier's per-box limit), and carrier
   choice.
4. Generate and check carton labels against FBA's current label specification before printing.
5. Keep the full paper trail: bill of lading, carrier receipt, carton count: so a later lost-inventory claim has
   the evidence it needs.
6. Confirm the shipment against Amazon's inbound dashboard once it is marked received, and flag any discrepancy
   between what was sent and what was received.

## Checks
- The dimension limits used are the currently published ones, not a cached figure.
- The paper trail is complete before the shipment physically leaves.

## Output
{dimension_check, shipment_plan, carton_labels, paper_trail, receipt_confirmation}

## Example
Case dimensions checked against FBA's current oversize threshold: under by 2cm. Template reused from the last
shipment of the same SKU. 40 cartons, weight checked under the carrier's 25kg/box limit. Paper trail filed; receipt
confirmed 6 days later with a 2-unit discrepancy flagged for a claim.

# Sequence an Amazon account, Brand Registry and launch

## Purpose
Account setup, trademark filing, Brand Registry enrolment and launch-week execution have a strict order: doing
them out of order (enrolling Brand Registry before the trademark is filed, for instance) causes rejections and
weeks of delay. This skill enforces the correct sequence.

## Steps
1. Get the Amazon seller account, business entity, payout details and identity verification right the first time
: a rejected or later-flagged account costs far more time than a careful first submission.
2. Sequence trademark filing before listing creation; Brand Registry cannot be enrolled without a filed trademark,
   so this step must complete first.
3. Once the trademark is filed and the listing (built via PROD-W22) is live, enrol Brand Registry.
4. Turn on the Storefront and Subscribe & Save benefits Brand Registry unlocks, confirming both are actually live,
   not just eligible.
5. Concentrate real demand into the first launch weeks by aligning stock arrival and PPC campaign start to the same
   date, and build a pre-launch audience where the platform's rules allow it.
6. Protect a novel product against copycats from day one: watermark product images, and file for design protection
   where the product is genuinely novel.

## Checks
- No step in the sequence is attempted before its prerequisite is confirmed complete.
- Stock and PPC go live on the same date, never staggered by more than a day.

## Output
{account_status, trademark_status, brand_registry_status, launch_plan, protection_checklist}

## Example
Account verified on first submission (2 weeks). Trademark filed before listing creation. Listing built and live.
Brand Registry enrolled once both prerequisites confirmed. Launch week: stock arrived and PPC campaign started the
same day; a pre-launch waitlist built the prior 2 weeks.

# Monitor marketplace health: reviews, account health, Buy Box

## Purpose
A policy notice ignored for a week can become a suspension; an unauthorized reseller undercutting on price can
erode a brand's own margin and trust. This skill runs the standing weekly health check that keeps both from
becoming a surprise.

## Steps
1. Request product reviews only through the platform's own permitted request mechanism: never an incentivised or
   off-platform review ask, which risks policy action against the account.
2. Contest any feedback that is misplaced (attached to the wrong product) or violates the platform's own feedback
   policy, through the platform's formal dispute process.
3. Check the Account Health dashboard every single week without exception, so a new policy notice is caught the
   week it appears, not discovered a month later as a suspension.
4. Check who holds the Buy Box across every marketplace listing, and check unauthorised reseller pricing against
   the brand's own MAP (minimum advertised price) policy.
5. Flag any MAP or price-integrity problem to the founder for a decision, rather than changing the brand's own
   price unilaterally in response.

## Checks
- Every review request uses a platform-permitted method.
- No price is changed by this agent in response to a MAP issue; it is always flagged to the founder.

## Output
{review_requests[], account_health_status, buy_box_report, map_violation_flags[]}

## Example
Account Health: clear, no new notices this week. Buy Box: held on 8 of 9 active listings; the 9th lost to an
unauthorized reseller pricing 12% below the brand's MAP: flagged for the founder rather than matching the price.

# Diagnose Amazon performance and plan growth

## Purpose
A sales drop on Amazon has at least two very different causes: fewer people seeing the listing, or fewer people
buying once they see it: and confusing the two leads to the wrong fix. This skill forces that split before any
other conclusion, and keeps growth responses inside Amazon's own compliant tools.

## Steps
1. Split any sales change into a traffic component and a conversion component, using Business Reports data, before
   drawing any conclusion about the product.
2. Check attribution (is the traffic even coming from where it looks like) and seasonality (is this the normal
   pattern for this time of year) before calling a product a failure based on a raw sales number.
3. Respond only with Amazon's own compliant promotion tools: Lightning Deals, Coupons, Amazon-native ad formats: 
   never an outside workaround that risks a policy violation.
4. Decide whether to add a second SKU based on the diagnosis, not on a hunch, and test smaller situational growth
   levers (FBM to FBA conversion, Small and Light enrolment, a design-vendor bake-off, Amazon Live) each with a
   defined read set before the test starts.
5. Write the one-page memo behind any decision to add or expand the Amazon channel.

## Checks
- The traffic/conversion split happens before any conclusion about the product itself.
- Every growth-lever test has its read defined before the test starts, never decided after seeing results.

## Output
{diagnosis{traffic_change, conversion_change}, promotion_response, growth_tests[], channel_memo}

## Example
Sales down 22% week over week. Diagnosis: traffic down 3% (normal seasonality), conversion down 19%: points to a
listing or price issue, not a demand problem. Response: a compliant Coupon test with a defined 2-week read, not an
off-platform discount code.

# Build, validate and audit the catalogue feed

## Purpose
Media buyer and Organic both depend on one clean feed to plug into shopping ads and marketplace channels, and a
broken image or a duplicate SKU discovered by a channel's own rejection wastes a cycle that a standing audit would
have caught first.

## Steps
1. Keep one clean master product feed: titles, images, prices, availability, and GTIN, with no duplicate SKU and
   no missing GTIN.
2. Validate the feed against each destination channel's own current schema before handing it off: a schema that
   worked last month may have changed.
3. Hand the validated feed to Media buyer and Organic, and confirm it loaded without error on their side.
4. Run a standing audit across every channel's live listings for broken images, missing attributes, and duplicate
   SKUs that may have crept in independently of the feed.
5. Check for the brand's own price mismatch between its site and each marketplace, flagging any gap rather than
   silently reconciling it.
6. Check every new product image and video against each channel's own size, crop and content rule before it is
   pushed, since an Instacart thumbnail and an Amazon main image have entirely different requirements (india: a Blinkit
   thumbnail; markets: IN).

## Checks
- The feed has zero duplicate SKUs and zero missing GTINs before handoff.
- A price mismatch is always flagged, never quietly auto-corrected.
- Image and video specs are checked before push, not discovered via a channel's rejection.

## Output
{master_feed, validation_report, quality_audit_report, price_mismatch_report, asset_spec_flags[]}

## Example
Feed validated clean against Amazon's, Walmart's and Instacart's current schemas. Weekly audit found 3 SKUs with a
broken image link on one marketplace and a $2 price mismatch between site and Walmart: both flagged, neither
auto-corrected. India: the same audit flags a ₹20 price mismatch between site and Flipkart instead (markets: IN).

# Onboard a brand on rapid-delivery and quick-commerce platforms

## Purpose
Rapid-delivery/quick-commerce onboarding requires a specific document set and each platform runs its own review
process and its own unit-economics validation window (commonly around 90 days) before the brand is judged to be
worth investing in further. Missing a required document is the most common cause of onboarding delay. India: the
same job onboards to Blinkit, Zepto or Instamart with GST and FSSAI documents instead (markets: IN).

## Steps
1. Assemble the business licence, resale certificate, UPC/GS1 barcode and packaging documents the platform's own
onboarding checklist requires, confirming every item is present before submission (India: GST registration, FSSAI
licence, PAN, bank and GS1 barcode documents instead; markets: IN).
2. Submit through the platform's own onboarding channel (Instacart Retailer/CPG portal, DoorDash Marketplace,
Gopuff vendor channel; india: Blinkit Seller App, Zepto category-manager channel, Instamart seller portal), never
a workaround or a third-party shortcut.
3. Track the document review status and respond to any query the platform raises within its stated window.
4. Prepare the initial catalogue listing using the matching platform listing skill.
5. Confirm the platform's own unit-economics validation window and what it requires the brand to demonstrate
during it.
6. Get the brand live and confirm the first order flows correctly end to end before calling onboarding complete.

## Checks
- Every document the platform's checklist requires is present before submission.
- The validation window and its specific requirement are both logged, not assumed.

## Output
{document_packet, review_status, initial_listing, validation_window, go_live_confirmation}

## Example
Documents assembled: business licence, resale certificate, UPC registration, packaging compliance declaration.
Submitted through Instacart's Retailer portal. First order confirmed to flow correctly on day 12 of a stated
90-day validation window. India: the same brand's Blinkit onboarding instead used GST, FSSAI licence and GS1
barcode documents (markets: IN).

# Manage rapid-delivery ad credits and dark-store fill rate

## Purpose
Rapid-delivery/quick-commerce platforms typically report ROAS on list/MRP price, which overstates real return by
30 to 50 percent; judging ad spend on that number leads to bad decisions. And a dark-store stockout triggers an
algorithmic ranking penalty that takes real time to recover from, so it needs daily, not weekly, attention.

## Steps
1. Spend each platform's ad tools deliberately rather than leaving credits unused, and pull back spend for a SKU
once its organic search ranking improves and stops needing paid support.
2. Recompute ROAS from actual transaction value, never the platform's own list/MRP-based default, before judging
whether spend is working.
3. Negotiate peak promotional windows (BFCM, Prime Day, Q4 holidays; India: the festive calendar; markets: IN)
ahead of the calendar date, since terms secured early are typically better than what is available once the rush
begins.
4. Watch stock levels across the dark-store network daily, the way a merchandiser walks the shelf, and flag a
stockout before it triggers the platform's own algorithmic ranking penalty, which is slow to recover from once
triggered.

## Checks
- Every ROAS figure used for a decision is recomputed from transaction value, never quoted from the platform's
  list/MRP-based dashboard number.
- A fill-rate flag is raised before the ranking-penalty window closes, not after the penalty has already applied.

## Output
{ad_spend_plan, roas_recomputed, promo_terms, dark_store_report, stockout_flags[]}

## Example
Platform-reported ROAS: 4.2x (list-price-based). Recomputed from transaction value: 2.9x: spend plan adjusted down
for the weakest SKU. Dark-store report: 2 of 40 stores below reorder threshold, flagged same day, ahead of the
platform's ranking-penalty window.

# Track FDA, net-quantity, state licence and EPR compliance

## Purpose
FDA facility registration, Fair Packaging and Labeling Act net-quantity declarations, state licensing (cosmetics,
food, supplements) and state EPR packaging filing are each recurring, concrete obligations that a brand either
tracks deliberately or handles ad hoc under deadline pressure. This skill keeps one register instead of several
scattered across people's memory. India: the same register tracks Legal Metrology (Packaged Commodities)
registration, an FSSAI licence and India's EPR plastic-packaging rules instead (markets: IN, reads null for US
brands).

## Steps
1. Keep one register listing which SKUs require FDA facility registration or a state cosmetics/food/supplement
licence, based on their actual category (India: Legal Metrology state registration or an FSSAI licence; markets:
IN).
2. Track each licence's current validity window, so an expiry is known well ahead of the date, not discovered
after it lapses.
3. Flag the relabelling a SKU needs on any formula, claim or price change: net quantity, ingredients and any
Prop 65 warning (India: on any MRP or GST change, keeping the original MRP visible as the rule requires; markets:
IN).
4. Register the brand's packaging under the relevant state's EPR rules (Oregon, California, Colorado, Maine;
India: under India's EPR rules; markets: IN), and track the annual filing deadline and recycling-target
obligation.
5. Flag when a shortfall against the recycling target means the brand needs to buy EPR credits, stating the
shortfall amount specifically.

## Checks
- Every licence's validity window reflects a checked, current status, never an assumption that it is still valid.
- A relabelling flag fires on every formula/claim/price change, not only when a licence comes up for renewal.

## Output
{licence_register[], relabelling_flags[], epr_status, epr_shortfall_flag}

## Example
Licence register: 14 of 18 SKUs require a state cosmetics licence or FDA registration, all current. One state
licence expiring in 45 days, flagged to the founder. A recent formula change on 3 SKUs triggered a relabelling
flag. Oregon EPR filing on track; no shortfall this cycle. India: the same brand's Legal Metrology/FSSAI register
and EPR filing run the equivalent check (markets: IN).

# Reconcile a settlement source

## Purpose
Every outside source (a gateway, a marketplace, a card network dispute, an ad platform, or for an India-selling brand a COD courier) pays, bills or reverses money on its own schedule and its own math. This skill is the dispatcher: it picks the right sub-skill by source and never lets a gap get filed away as rounding.

## Steps
1. Pull the source's statement for the period.
2. Match `select_by.source` to gateway, marketplace, ad-platform-invoices, chargebacks, or cod-courier (India option) and hand off to that child skill.
3. Run `money.reconciliation` with the source's own unbundling rule (fee, commission, facilitator sales tax or GST/TCS on fee, refund, shipping fee as separate lines).
4. Match the unbundled total to the actual bank credit or the actual ad spend logged.
5. Name a cause for every gap over a small tolerance.
6. Draft the journal entry from the unbundled lines, one entry per settlement.

## Checks
- No gap is left unexplained.
- Facilitator sales tax (or TCS and GST for India) on fees are always their own lines.
- The matched total ties to a real bank credit, not an assumption.

## Output
A reconciliation table with source, period, matched total, gap total, named gap causes and draft journal entries.

## Example
A Meta invoice of $4,230 for the month is matched against $4,185 logged in the spend dashboard. The $45 gap is named: a late-arriving credit from the prior invoice, not rounding.

# Reconcile payment gateway settlement

## Purpose
A gateway payout is never the same as gross sales. This skill unbundles every payout into its real parts so the books never show one lump deposit.

## Steps
1. Pull the settlement file for the period and the matching bank statement.
2. For each payout, unbundle gross sale, gateway fee, refund, sales tax charged on the fee (GST on the fee for India-selling brands), and any FX adjustment for cross-border payments.
3. Match the net figure to the actual bank credit.
4. Age any payout not credited inside the gateway's stated settlement window (typically T+1 to T+3).
5. Draft the journal entry with each unbundled line as its own account.

## Checks
- Fee and tax on fee never merge into one line.
- FX adjustment is separated from the fee, never hidden inside it.
- An aged payout carries a day count, not a vague 'pending' label.

## Output
One row per payout: gross, fee, tax on fee, refund, FX adjustment, net, bank match status, age in days.

## Example
A Stripe payout of $1,180 unbundles to $1,225 gross sale, minus $21 fee, minus $4 tax on the fee, minus $20 refunds, net $1,180, matched to the bank credit dated 2 days later.

# Reconcile marketplace settlement

## Purpose
Marketplace settlements bury commission, fees, facilitator sales tax and refunds inside one payout figure. This skill pulls them apart and checks the marketplace charged what it agreed to.

## Steps
1. Pull the settlement report and the marketplace's 1099-K or facilitator tax statement for the period (TCS certificate for India-selling brands).
2. Unbundle commission, fixed fee, shipping fee, marketplace-facilitator sales tax withheld, and refunds (TCS under Section 52 and GST on fees, for India).
3. Match facilitator sales tax withheld (or TCS deducted, for India) in the settlement to the marketplace's own statement or certificate.
4. Match every refund line in the settlement to an actual return in the order data.
5. Check the commission rate charged against the brand's agreed rate card by category.
6. Flag any mismatch with the exact order or SKU it came from.

## Checks
- Facilitator sales tax (or TCS for India) is never assumed correct; it is matched to the marketplace's own statement.
- A refund with no matching return is flagged, not silently accepted.
- The commission rate check is per category, since rates vary by category.

## Output
One row per payout with gross, commission, fixed fee, shipping fee, facilitator tax, refunds, net and a rate-card check result.

## Example
An Amazon payout shows 15 percent commission on a category the rate card sets at 12.5 percent; the 2.5 point gap is flagged against the specific SKU category before the settlement is booked.

# Reconcile COD cash and courier remittance

## Purpose
COD cash sits with the courier until it is remitted. This skill ages that gap by courier so a slow remittance is caught before it becomes a cash problem instead of an accounting afterthought.

## Steps
1. Pull the courier's own collection report and remittance report for the period.
2. Match collected cash per order to the remittance that eventually lands in the bank.
3. Age every gap in days, by courier, against that courier's own stated SLA cycle.
4. For any remittance stuck past the SLA, build the escalation note: the order IDs, the amount, and the SLA clause it breaches.
5. Feed the unremitted total into the cash forecast as a receivable, never as cash in hand.

## Checks
- Aging never blends couriers together; each courier has its own SLA cycle.
- An escalation cites the SLA clause by name, not a general complaint.
- Unremitted COD lowers the cash forecast's available cash, it does not inflate it.

## Output
A table by courier: collected, remitted, gap, age in days, SLA cycle days, and an escalation flag with order IDs where the gap exceeds the SLA.

## Example
Courier X's SLA is a 7-day remittance cycle; an 82,000 rupee batch sits at 11 days. The escalation names the 34 order IDs and cites the 7-day clause in the courier's own service agreement.

## Market note
This skill applies only to an India-selling brand that runs cash on delivery. It reads null for a US-only brand, whose payout reconciliation runs through money/reconcile/gateway and money/reconcile/marketplace, with money/reconcile/chargebacks handling disputes.

# Reconcile ad platform invoices to logged spend

## Purpose
Ad platforms bill on their own cycle, which rarely lines up cleanly with a calendar month or with the currency the dashboard reports in. This skill catches the gap before it distorts the P&L's marketing cost line.

## Steps
1. Pull the platform's invoice for the billing period.
2. Pull the dashboard's logged spend for the matching period, as a period total, never an average of daily figures.
3. Compare the two totals directly.
4. If they differ, check for a billing-cycle boundary mismatch, a currency conversion difference, or a credit or refund applied by the platform.
5. Name the exact cause; never file the gap as unexplained variance.

## Checks
- Comparison always uses period totals, never daily averages.
- A currency conversion gap states the rate used on each side.
- The gap becomes a line in the platform-to-books reconciliation, not a silent write-off.

## Output
One line per platform per period: invoiced amount, logged amount, gap, and the named cause.

## Example
Meta's invoice covers the 3rd to the 2nd of the next month, while the dashboard reports calendar months; the resulting $620 shift is named as a billing-cycle boundary, not a spend discrepancy.

# Reconcile and represent chargebacks and disputes

## Purpose
A chargeback or dispute is a reversal, not a return: it goes through the card network or PayPal, on their own deadline, and needs its own evidence packet. This skill treats it as a first-class reconciliation source, the same as a gateway or marketplace payout, and never lets a filing deadline slip.

## Steps
1. Pull every open dispute from each gateway or processor (Shopify Payments, Stripe, PayPal), with its reason code, amount and deadline.
2. Assemble the evidence packet the specific reason code calls for: proof of delivery, customer communication, IP/device match, policy acceptance.
3. File representment before the deadline.
4. Track whether the representment won or lost, and log the reason code either way.
5. Roll the result into the win-rate report by reason code and gateway.

## Checks
- No dispute is missing a filing deadline.
- The evidence packet is built for the specific reason code, not a one-size packet.
- Win rate is tracked by reason code and gateway, never blended into one number.

## Output
One row per dispute: gateway, reason code, amount, deadline, evidence packet, and outcome once resolved.

## Example
A Stripe dispute with reason code 'product not received' gets a packet built from the shipping carrier's delivery confirmation and the customer's own delivery-confirmation email, filed two days before the ten-day deadline.

## Market note
An India-selling brand runs the same skill for a UPI dispute, assembling the OTP log alongside delivery proof and support chat.

# Audit a tracking surface

# Purpose
GA4, Meta pixel and CAPI, Google Ads and server-side tagging each drift on their own schedule. This skill is the dispatcher that sends the audit to the right surface-specific checklist and never applies a fix itself.

## Steps
1. Match `select_by.surface` to ga4, meta-capi, google-ads or server-events and hand off to that child skill.
2. Pull the surface's current live configuration, dated.
3. Run the fixed checklist for that surface.
4. Verify every store event (purchase, add to cart, lead) maps to that surface's own standard or key event, with value passed through.
5. Test the live setup in the surface's own debug tool (DebugView, Test Events, or the Google Ads diagnostics tab).
6. Build the ranked fix list: current setting, proposed setting, and who applies it.

## Checks
- Every checklist item returns pass, fail or unavailable, never skipped.
- No tracking configuration is changed; only the fix list is produced.
- A fix names the surface it touches.

## Output
Surface, checklist result, event mapping table, debug test result and a ranked fix list.

## Example
A GA4 audit finds `page_view` still marked as a key event, inflating the key-event count; the fix list names the exact setting to unmark, for a person with GA4 admin access to apply.

# Audit GA4 tracking

## Purpose
Catch broken or misconfigured GA4 settings before they corrupt a report someone reads with confidence.

## Steps
1. Confirm one property exists per customer journey, not one property doing double duty.
2. Check timezone, data retention window, and that internal and staff traffic is filtered out.
3. Confirm consent mode gating matches the live consent banner's states.
4. Confirm enhanced measurement is on and ecommerce parameters (item, value, currency) are present on purchase events.
5. Confirm key events are the real conversion actions; `page_view` is never marked as one.
6. Fire a real test session and confirm it appears correctly in DebugView.

## Checks
- One property per journey.
- Internal traffic is filtered, confirmed by a live check.
- No `page_view` marked as a key event.

## Output
A checklist result per item plus the DebugView test outcome.

## Example
DebugView shows a purchase event firing with `value: 0` because the ecommerce parameter was not mapped from the checkout's order total; the fix list names the exact parameter to map.

# Audit Meta pixel and CAPI

## Purpose
A browser pixel and a server-side CAPI event for the same purchase must dedup correctly, or Meta double-counts conversions and the reported ROAS is wrong.

## Steps
1. Read dataset quality and event match quality with the read-only Meta MCP tools (`ads_pixel_event_read`, `ads_get_dataset_quality`, `ads_get_dataset_stats`). Never call a write tool.
2. Check that pixel and CAPI events for the same action share the same event ID for deduplication.
3. Confirm every store event maps to a Meta standard event (Purchase, AddToCart, Lead) with value and currency passed.
4. Confirm consent gating blocks the event until consent is given, matching the banner.
5. Fire a real test event and confirm it appears in Meta's Test Events tool.

## Checks
- Dedup is confirmed by matching event IDs, never assumed from setup screenshots.
- Event match quality is read from the platform, never estimated.
- Only read tools are used; this skill never creates, updates or activates anything.

## Output
Dedup check, event match quality score, standard-event mapping table, consent gating check and test event result.

## Example
Event match quality reads low because the CAPI event sends no phone or email hash; the fix list names the exact hashed parameter to add server-side.

# Audit Google Ads conversion tracking

## Purpose
A wrong or duplicated primary conversion action skews every bid strategy built on it.

## Steps
1. Confirm exactly one primary purchase conversion action is set; flag any duplicate or secondary action miscounted as primary.
2. Confirm enhanced conversions pass the real order value through, not an estimated average order value.
3. Pick the tracking route (native app SDK, GTM, or server-side container) that matches the brand's current spend level; a small brand rarely needs full server-side tagging yet.
4. Check for conflicting or overlapping conversion actions counting the same purchase twice.
5. Confirm the setup in the Google Ads diagnostics tab with a live test conversion.

## Checks
- One primary purchase action, confirmed live.
- Order value is the real total, never an estimate.
- The tracking route is justified by the brand's spend level, not left as whatever was set up first.

## Output
Primary action check, enhanced conversions check, chosen tracking route with justification, duplicate action check and diagnostics result.

## Example
Two conversion actions are both marked primary after a past migration; the fix list names which one to demote so bidding does not double-count purchases.

# Audit server-side tag management

## Purpose
GA4 and Meta audits check their own tags. This skill checks the container that fires them, since a broken container structure breaks every tag inside it at once.

## Steps
1. Map the full container structure: triggers, variables, and every tag firing from it.
2. Check the server-side tagging setup specifically: which events route through a server container versus the browser, and whether that split still matches the brand's spend level.
3. Confirm consent mode gating is applied at the container level, not per tag inconsistently.
4. Find duplicate tags firing the same event twice, and dead tags pointing at a destination that no longer exists.
5. Confirm the container's last change matches the last known-good state after any recent site or app change.

## Checks
- The container is audited as a whole, not tag by tag with no view of the structure.
- Dead tags are named specifically, not left firing silently and wasting event quota.
- Consent gating is checked at the container level.

## Output
Container structure check, server-side routing check, consent gating check and a named dead-tag list.

## Example
A tag left over from a discontinued email platform still fires on every checkout page; it is named in the dead-tag list for removal.

# Build the P&L ladder and run the close checklist

## Purpose
Turn raw order and cost exports into a labeled, comparable P&L ladder, and confirm the close is actually complete before anyone reads the numbers.

## Steps
1. Apply the brand's fixed decision tree for what counts as COGS, cost of delivery, marketing cost and OPEX.
2. Build the ladder line by line from gross revenue down to net profit.
3. Run the close checklist: bank reconciliations complete, accruals booked, inventory valuation current, deferred revenue correctly held.
4. Diff this month's ladder against last month's and name the single biggest driver of change.

## Checks
- Every ladder line traces to a source document or a reconciliation output.
- No cost appears in both COGS and OPEX.
- A percent-of-revenue column sits next to every ladder line.

## Output
The P&L ladder, the close checklist with a pass or fail per item, and one paragraph naming the biggest change.

## Example
Net profit percent drops 3 points month over month; the diff names the driver as a spike in carrier shipping fees, not a vague 'costs went up'.

# Compute contribution margin by scope

## Purpose
Nobody should guess what a margin number includes. This skill always states which layer of cost it has subtracted.

## Steps
1. Compute CM1: revenue minus COGS.
2. Compute CM2: CM1 minus delivery and fulfillment cost.
3. Compute CM3: CM2 minus the marketing cost attributed to that scope.
4. Attach the scope label (SKU, basket or channel) to every figure.
5. Rank SKUs and classify each as champion, hidden gem, growth driver or underperformer, using contribution and cash tied up in inventory.

## Checks
- Every number states CM1, CM2 or CM3 explicitly.
- Classification uses both contribution and cash tied up, never contribution alone.

## Output
CM1, CM2, CM3 for the requested scope, plus a SKU classification tag where the scope is SKU.

## Example
A best-selling SKU shows strong CM1 but is classified underperformer once CM3 accounts for the paid spend driving most of its sales.

# Compute true customer profitability

## Purpose
A customer who buys often but returns often, or costs a lot in support tickets, may be worth less than a quieter customer. This skill puts every real cost against revenue before anyone calls someone a VIP.

## Steps
1. Pull support-ticket cost per contact, return and refund cost, shipping cost and discount cost for each customer.
2. Subtract all four from revenue, in code, to get true profitability.
3. Compare true profitability to the customer's current loyalty tier.
4. Flag any customer whose tier does not match their true profitability rank.

## Checks
- No cost bucket is estimated; a missing one is marked unavailable, never zero.
- The comparison to loyalty tier uses true profit, never raw revenue.

## Output
A table per customer: revenue, each cost bucket, true profit, current tier, and a mismatch flag.

## Example
A customer with the highest revenue this year is flagged for a tier downgrade once true profit accounts for an 18 percent return rate and 6 support tickets.

# Price or promo from a profit target

## Purpose
Price bottom-up from a real profit target, never top-down from a keystone guess, and never let a promo go live without knowing its true break-even.

## Steps
1. Read the brand's stated net-profit target for the SKU or line.
2. For a price: solve the waterfall from landed cost through fees, shipping, returns and marketing cost to the shelf price that hits the target.
3. For a promo: model the real cost shape of the specific mechanic (percent-off, BOGO, gift-with-purchase, flash sale), not a flat assumption.
4. Run a break-even go/no-go check, or a margin stress-test for a new price.
5. Once live, stress-test the price against 60 to 90 days of real sell-through.

## Checks
- The profit target always comes from the brand record.
- Every waterfall line between cost and price is shown, none skipped or merged.

## Output
The full waterfall or promo cost model, the recommended price or the break-even volume, and the stress-test result once available.

## Example
A proposed BOGO on a 40 percent margin SKU breaks even only above a 22 percent lift in units; the gate returns no-go until a lift test confirms that volume is realistic.

# Build and monitor the 13-week cash forecast

## Purpose
Find the lowest cash point before it happens, and never let an inventory plan assume cash that will not be there.

## Steps
1. Pull bank balance, payroll calendar, ad spend plan, inventory on order and supplier lead times.
2. Build the rolling 13-week forecast week by week.
3. Reconcile this month's profit to free cash flow and check the 4 known cash traps (inventory build, tax timing, prepaid deposits, return timing).
4. Flag the lowest projected week at least 3 weeks ahead, with a sensitivity range.
5. Roll inventory forward against supplier lead time, targeting days-of-inventory to that lead time.
6. Track the cash conversion cycle (days inventory plus days receivable minus days payable) as one number with its 3 parts shown.

## Checks
- Inventory is never modeled to go negative.
- Profit and cash are reconciled explicitly, not assumed equal.
- The lowest point is flagged with enough lead time to act.

## Output
The 13-week table, the lowest-cash-week flag with sensitivity, the inventory cash plan and the cash conversion cycle.

## Example
Week 9 is flagged as the lowest point due to a supplier deposit and a state sales-tax payment landing the same week; the flag fires in week 5, giving 4 weeks to arrange a bridge.

# Compare financing options against the cash forecast

## Purpose
A financing decision made against the actual 13-week forecast, at the real cost of capital, not the advertised rate.

## Steps
1. Pull the current cash forecast and the lowest-cash flag if one exists.
2. Compare a line of credit, inventory financing and revenue-based financing against reference cost-of-capital rates for each.
3. For a hard-to-source or hard-to-fund launch, widen the search to crowdfunding, private capital and manufacturer referrals, and look for a cheap way to prototype before any commitment.
4. Stress-test the repayment schedule of the leading option against the brand's own slowest historical month, not a generic haircut.

## Checks
- Every option is shown at its real annualized cost of capital.
- The stress test uses the brand's own sales history, not an assumed decline.

## Output
A comparison table of options with real cost of capital, and a repayment stress-test result for the leading option.

## Example
A revenue-based advance's headline '8 percent fee' works out to a 34 percent annualized cost once the repayment period is short; the comparison states the annualized figure next to the headline one.

# Assemble the data room and investor/lender reporting pack

## Purpose
Package the numbers that already exist (P&L, cash, cohort economics) into the shape a lender or investor asks for, without inventing a new deliverable.

## Steps
1. Pull the current P&L ladder, cash forecast, CAC/LTV report and cap table.
2. Assemble the data room with every document dated.
3. Produce the monthly update and check loan covenants explicitly as met or breached.
4. Produce the quarterly board deck's financial section from the same source numbers, never a separate estimate.

## Checks
- Every document in the room carries a version date.
- Covenant status is stated plainly, never implied by a number sitting near a threshold.

## Output
The current data room, the covenant compliance status, and the board deck's financial pages.

## Example
A loan covenant requires a minimum current ratio of 1.2; this month's ratio of 1.15 is stated as breached, with the cash forecast page showing the path back above 1.2.

# Procure insurance cover and file claims

## Purpose
Match real coverage to the brand's real risk, and never let a claim slip past the insurer's evidence requirements or the filing deadline.

## Steps
1. Identify the coverage types that apply: product liability, cyber, business owner's policy, and D&O once outside investors are involved.
2. Compare quotes on premium, deductible and exclusions together, never premium in isolation.
3. Track every active policy's renewal date and flag it at least 30 days ahead.
4. On a loss (transit, stock, cyber, product liability), assemble the claim with the exact evidence that insurer requires and track it through to resolution.

## Checks
- The quote comparison always shows deductible and exclusions next to premium.
- A claim always cites the specific policy clause it is filed under.

## Output
A coverage checklist, a quote comparison table, a renewal calendar, or a tracked claim file.

## Example
A cheaper cyber policy excludes ransomware payment cost; the comparison flags that exclusion even though its premium looks like the better deal.

# Report CAC, LTV, revenue forecast and the budget

## Purpose
One engine for the numbers that decide whether to spend the next marketing dollar, so every module uses the same screened order data and the same cohort definitions.

## Steps
1. Screen the order set for fraud and bot-driven orders before any cohort math runs.
2. Compute blended, media-only, paid and fully loaded CAC, each labeled.
3. Build first-order cohorts and compute CAC payback and LTGP:CAC against the metric contract's fixed bands.
4. Forecast new-customer and returning revenue from the spend-efficiency curve, cohort repeat rate and the dated marketing calendar as separate inputs.
5. For a subscription brand, build churn against the correct prior-period base and conservative lifetime estimates.
6. Build the annual OPEX budget sized to the brand's own profit target, separate from the rolling forecast.

## Checks
- LTV is gross profit, never revenue.
- No channel-level CAC substitutes for the blended finance number.
- A short sales history is regressed to the mean, never extrapolated in a straight line.

## Output
The requested module's report: CAC/LTV dashboard, revenue forecast with error bars, subscription unit economics, or the OPEX budget.

## Example
A channel with a great platform-reported ROAS shows a payback period of 11 months once fully loaded CAC and true cohort repeat rate are applied; the scale recommendation holds at current spend, not more.

# Evaluate a third-party attribution or MMM stack

## Purpose
Decide whether a paid tool (Triple Whale, Northbeam, Rockerbox or similar) earns its subscription cost against what the brand can already do with its own blended MER and lift tests.

## Steps
1. Pull the current attribution gap report showing where platform and GA4 or blended numbers disagree.
2. Pull the tool's real cost and its claimed accuracy improvement, cited to its own source and date.
3. Compare that claim against the brand's own current lift-test accuracy and blended-MER track record.
4. Recommend adopt, reject or park, stating the cost and the accuracy gap side by side.

## Checks
- A vendor's accuracy claim is never repeated as fact; it is labeled as a vendor claim to verify.
- The recommendation states the real cost against the brand's own current accuracy, not against a competitor's case study.

## Output
Tool name, cost, claimed accuracy gain, the brand's own current accuracy, and a recommendation.

## Example
A tool costing 2,400 dollars a month claims a 15 percent accuracy gain; the brand's own recent holdout tests already track within 8 percent of platform-reported ROAS, so the recommendation is park until the gap widens.

# Track US sales tax nexus and filing compliance (GST/HSN for India)

## Purpose
Track the mechanics that feed a state sales-tax filing (a GST filing for India-selling brands) so the brand's own accountant or filing service files correctly and on time; this skill tracks, it does not file.

## Steps
1. Build the SKU-to-product-tax-code map in Avalara or TaxJar and validate every category match (SKU-to-HSN/SAC map for India, where a wrong or short code is a common cause of e-invoice portal rejections).
2. Track sales-tax nexus and registration thresholds per state the brand sells into.
3. Prepare the return-ready sales and exemption data each state's filing needs (GSTR-1 and 3B inputs matched against GSTR-2B, for India).
4. Reconcile marketplace-facilitator sales tax and 1099-K totals against the credit or exclusion actually available (TCS collected under Section 52 and TDS deducted, for India).
5. India only: raise e-way bills for B2B dispatch and stock transfer above the threshold.
6. Check that every completed return or refund has a matching sales-tax credit memo issued and filed on time (a GST credit note, for India).

## Checks
- No SKU ships without a validated tax code.
- Facilitator sales tax (or TCS and GST on fees, for India) are always separate lines.
- A refund without a matching credit memo is flagged before the filing period closes.

## Output
The requested scope's result: tax-code map, nexus status, filing input pack, facilitator-credit reconciliation, credit-memo reconciliation, or (India only) e-way bill log.

## Example
A new SKU crosses economic nexus in a state before its first sale there is registered; the nexus tracker flags the state before the next filing deadline, avoiding an unregistered-collection gap.

## Market note
An India-selling brand runs the HSN/SAC, e-way bill and GSTR path instead, which reads null for a US-only brand.

# Maintain the fixed asset register and depreciation schedule

## Purpose
Keep one register of every asset the brand owns (equipment, fixtures, website build cost, packaging dies) so depreciation never gets estimated at year end.

## Steps
1. Log any new capital purchase with its date, cost and category.
2. Assign useful life from the brand's stated policy, not a one-off guess.
3. Run the month's depreciation for every asset in the register.
4. Update each asset's running balance.

## Checks
- Every asset carries purchase date, useful life and a running balance.
- No capital purchase this month is missing from the register.

## Output
The updated register with this month's depreciation line per asset.

## Example
A new packaging die purchased for $2,200 with a 3-year useful life adds about $60 of depreciation to this month's P&L ladder automatically.

# Run accounts payable, receivable, payroll and expense

## Purpose
One engine for the recurring cash-movement processes, so approval chains, payment terms and policy checks are applied the same way every cycle.

## Steps
1. For payable: capture every bill, match it to its PO and receipt, and route it through the approval chain by amount and vendor.
2. For receivable: invoice B2B and wholesale buyers on their agreed terms and run a structured dunning sequence on overdue accounts.
3. For payroll: process the cycle from the roster through Gusto or ADP, then prepare federal/state withholding and W-2/1099-NEC filings (PF, ESI, professional tax, TDS and Form 16 for India-selling brands).
4. For expense: apply the travel-and-expense policy to every receipt and card charge, then reconcile the card statement to the ledger.

## Checks
- No bill is scheduled for payment without completing its approval step.
- Payroll always shows the gross-to-net calculation, not the net figure alone.
- Every expense line is marked compliant or flagged against the written policy.

## Output
The requested process's result: AP approval queue and aging, AR aging and dunning log, payroll run and filing pack, or expense and card reconciliation.

## Example
A vendor bill routed for approval sits 4 days past the brand's own 3-day SLA for its amount tier; the aging report flags it by name before the vendor calls asking about it.

2. Reconcile what the affiliate network claims is owed against actual delivered, non-returned orders.

# Write and audit the UTM convention

## Purpose
A missing or inconsistent UTM turns paid traffic into fake organic or direct traffic in every report downstream. This skill keeps the convention fixed and the links clean.

## Steps
1. Write one convention for source, medium, campaign, content and term, with a fixed value set for each.
2. Audit every existing paid and owned link against that convention.
3. List every non-conforming link with its exact fix.
4. Clean the channel table of fake organic or direct rows traced to a broken UTM, before it is published.

## Checks
- Every UTM parameter has a documented, fixed set of allowed values.
- No channel report goes out with a known UTM leak still unflagged.

## Output
The convention document, the link audit table, and the cleaned channel table.

## Example
A large chunk of 'direct' traffic in GA4 traces to an email campaign sent without any UTM; the cleaned table reclassifies it and the audit flags the sending tool's default settings as the cause.

# Reconcile attribution models and order counts

## Purpose
Catch a bot-inflated session spike and a platform-versus-GA4 attribution disagreement before either one drives a budget decision.

## Steps
1. Cross-check GA4, Meta, Shopify and marketplace order counts against actual store orders for the period.
2. Flag any spike in one source's count that does not match store orders as a possible bot signal, and hand it to the security scan.
3. Report the gap between last-click and data-driven models, and between platform-reported and GA4-reported numbers, per channel.
4. Before a large reallocation, run or schedule a holdout test rather than trust the attribution gap alone.

## Checks
- Every order-count gap over 2 percent carries a named cause.
- The model gap is reported per channel, never collapsed into one number.

## Output
Order-count cross-check table, bot spike flag list, and the per-channel attribution gap report.

## Example
Meta reports 30 percent more sessions than GA4 for one campaign in a single week; the spike is flagged as a likely bot pattern and handed to the weekly security scan instead of being read as real interest.

Ask the customer directly when platform attribution and GA4 keep disagreeing, and turn the answer into a real number instead of an anecdote.

1. Draft the one question: how did you hear about us, in plain language.
2. Branch the answer options by product or customer type where the channel mix genuinely differs.

4. Turn the collected answers into a channel-share percentage, computed in code.

- The question stays one sentence.

A new influencer channel claims a large share of new customers on the platform's own dashboard; the survey after 400 responses shows only 9 percent of customers cite it, prompting a closer look at the platform's attribution window.

# Build and maintain the reporting dashboard set

## Purpose
Keep the numbers everyone reads trustworthy and current, and stop a dashboard from accumulating cards nobody trusts anymore.

## Steps
1. Compute the daily CM scoreboard, with the window ending on the last full day.
2. Compute the weekly profit memo inputs: CM, new versus returning revenue split from cohort data, variance against last week, and inventory risk.
3. Audit the standing dashboards (Shopify home cards, GA4 saved reports, budget scenario views) and name any card that no longer reads correctly.
4. Remove or flag unreliable cards, and add a card only when it answers a question someone actually asked recently.

## Checks
- Revenue, profit and cash never blend into one figure.
- Every card on the dashboard traces to a real question asked.

## Output
The daily scoreboard, the weekly memo inputs, or the cleaned dashboard set.

## Example
A GA4 card showing 'sessions by device' gets removed after nobody has referenced it in 3 months, replaced by a card the founder asked for twice: CM3 by channel this week versus last.

# Run structured hiring from scorecard to offer

## Purpose
Turn a hiring decision into a repeatable process with one governing metric per role, so a hire is never made on gut feel alone.

## Steps
1. Confirm the hire trigger fired: a stated number crossing a stated threshold.
2. Build the job description naming the silo, the artefacts owned, and one metric the role is judged on.
3. Set the comp band from the role library and the current OPEX budget.
4. Write an honest job ad matching the scorecard exactly, and a sourced interview question set tied to that one metric.
5. Score every candidate against the scorecard, citing the specific answer behind each score.
6. Recommend the top-scored candidate with the score gap to the next candidate, then stop.

## Checks
- The hire trigger is always a number.
- The scorecard names exactly one governing metric.
- No candidate is contacted by this skill; the founder makes every offer and rejection.

## Output
The stage's artefact: job description and scorecard, job ad, interview question set, or scored candidate table with a recommendation.

## Example
Two candidates score close on the interview set; the recommendation states the 4-point gap and which specific answer drove it, leaving the final call to the founder.

# Write SOPs, the handbook and offboarding checklists

## Purpose
Keep operating knowledge in a live document with a named owner, not in one person's head, and never leave an exit half-done.

## Steps
1. Spot when a procedure has been asked for a third time without a written SOP.
2. Write the SOP: purpose, numbered steps with the tool used at each, and the check before it counts as done.
3. Assign one named owner and a freshness date.
4. Keep the handbook current: leave, work-from-home, code of conduct, and the POSH policy section, and confirm every employee has acknowledged it.
5. On a resignation or termination notice, run the offboarding checklist: same-day access revocation, asset return, knowledge transfer, exit interview, final settlement.

## Checks
- Every SOP has exactly one named owner, never a team name.
- Access revocation on exit happens the same day, not the same week.

## Output
The requested document: a new SOP, the updated handbook with an acknowledgement log, or a completed offboarding checklist.

## Example
A third support agent asks how to handle a wrong-size return in the same week; the pattern triggers a written SOP instead of a fourth verbal explanation.

# Run a competitive vendor or 3PL RFP

## Purpose
Select and hold vendors to a real, written standard instead of a single quote and a handshake.

## Steps
1. Run the RFP against at least 3 candidate vendors.
2. Run a facility visit for a 3PL, or a reference check for an agency.
3. Put the SLA in writing with a numeric target and a stated consequence for a miss.
4. Audit every incoming invoice against the SLA and the RFP-agreed rate.
5. Score the vendor on a fixed scorecard computed from the SLA data.

## Checks
- At least 3 vendors are compared before a selection.
- Every SLA line has a numeric target and a named consequence.

## Output
The RFP comparison, the written SLA, the invoice audit result, and the vendor scorecard.

## Example
A 3PL's invoice bills a pick-and-pack fee 12 percent above the RFP-agreed rate for 6 straight weeks; the audit flags the exact line before it becomes a pattern nobody caught.

# Govern SaaS renewals, contracts, vendor risk and freelancers

## Purpose
Keep tool spend matched to revenue stage, stop a bad clause from getting signed, and never let a vendor touch customer data without a signed agreement.

## Steps
1. Audit the store's software spend against its current revenue stage; flag anything added too early, like an ERP for a brand that does not need one yet.
2. Watch every SaaS contract's auto-renew date and usage data, and draft a renegotiation or cancellation email citing the brand's own usage before the notice window closes.
3. Before a new SaaS tool, ESP, 3PL or agency gets data access, run the standard risk questionnaire and confirm a data-processing agreement is signed.
4. Run every incoming contract (NDA, MSA, vendor agreement, employment agreement) through the redline checklist.
5. Run a freelancer or contractor engagement's full lifecycle: scope of work, IP assignment, rate agreement, milestone invoicing, and renewal or offboarding.

## Checks
- No new system is proposed without a named owner.
- No vendor gets customer or payment data access without a signed DPA confirmed.
- IP assignment is explicit in every freelance engagement.

## Output
The requested scope's result: tooling audit, renewal watch and draft email, risk assessment, redlined contract, or freelancer engagement record.

## Example
A SaaS tool's usage drops to 20 percent of licensed seats 3 months before renewal; the draft cancellation email cites that exact usage number rather than a general request to lower the price.

# Plan CS capacity and handle CCPA/CPRA data-subject requests (DPDP for India)

## Purpose
Size support to the forecast, not the last headcount, and protect a customer's CCPA/CPRA rights (DPDP rights for an India-selling brand) across every system that holds their data.

## Steps
1. Staff CS tiers from the sales forecast curve and track cost per ticket by tier.
2. Define what counts as a complex ticket before it gets routed to a higher tier.
3. When resolution time rises, trace the cause upstream instead of just adding headcount.
4. On a CCPA/CPRA access, deletion or opt-out request (a DPDP access or erasure request, for India), find every system holding that person's data: ESP, helpdesk, loyalty, subscription, order records.
5. Assemble the data for an access request, or prepare the deletion/erasure plan across every located system, respecting any legal retention obligation.
6. Confirm the response goes out inside the statutory deadline and log the request.

## Checks
- Staffing scales with the forecast curve.
- Every connected system is checked for a data-subject request; none are skipped.
- A deletion or erasure never removes data needed for an open legal or tax obligation.

## Output
The requested task's result: a CS staffing plan with cost per ticket, or a completed data-subject response with its system-by-system data map.

## Example
A deletion request would delete an order record still needed for a live sales-tax audit trail (a GST audit trail for India); the plan erases the customer's marketing and support data while retaining the order record with a stated legal reason.

# Run the weekly fraud, bot and abuse scan

## Purpose
Catch card-testing, bot traffic, return abuse and domain impersonation early, with friction placed at checkout and account changes, never at ordinary browsing.

## Steps
1. Rebuild the bot and AI-agent traffic baseline by agent, endpoint and intent, and re-score risk tiers continuously.
2. Check for card-testing bursts (clusters of small failed authorizations) and review AVS/CVV/3DS settings against the false-decline rate.
3. Set the chargeback alert threshold below the processor's own flag level, and set step-up verification triggers for repeat abuse (prepayment triggers for repeat COD refusers, for India-selling brands).
4. Detect return and refund abuse: wardrobing, serial high-return customers, refunds without a matching return.
5. Watch the domain registrar lock status, DNS for dangling records, and lookalike domains or counterfeit listings.

## Checks
- No rule relies on User-Agent alone.
- Fraud caught is always tracked alongside the false-decline rate.

## Output
The traffic baseline, fraud and return-abuse flags, the domain watch result, and a ranked weekly fix list.

## Example
A burst of 40 small authorizations under $1 each from the same IP range is flagged as card-testing before any of them succeed at a full-value order.

# Run the monthly auth, web-app and backup audit

## Purpose
Confirm the controls that stop an account takeover or a site defect from becoming a real incident, and prove a backup actually restores.

## Steps
1. Audit login, session and MFA design: 2FA or passkeys for every admin, session-cookie attributes, password hashing and rate limiting, and enumeration prevention on login and reset flows.
2. Audit storefront and checkout code for XSS, injection, CSRF, clickjacking, CORS and postMessage defects.
3. Confirm daily versioned backups exist in 3 separated locations with a ransomware-safe, offline copy.
4. Test a restore end to end this month, not just confirm the backup exists.
5. Update the unified incident runbook covering breach, skimmer and ransomware scenarios.

## Checks
- 2FA is confirmed by a live check, not assumed from a settings screenshot.
- A restore test actually opens a restored file; it is not just a scheduled job that ran.

## Output
The auth audit, the web-app defect list with a developer fix list, the backup and restore test result, and the updated runbook.

## Example
A scheduled backup has run every night for 6 months but the restore test this month fails silently on a corrupted archive; the audit catches it before an actual incident would have.

# Run the quarterly four-pillar security audit

## Purpose
Run the recurring program with a named owner per pillar, so nothing waits for an incident to get checked.

## Steps
1. Map every staff role to only the admin areas it needs, run the full access audit, and confirm same-day offboarding for any recent exits.
2. Confirm GDPR/CCPA exposure by customer location and publish a privacy policy and consent banner covering AI-agent interactions.
3. Check SPF, DKIM, DMARC and BIMI on every sending domain and move DMARC from monitor-only toward enforced where safe.
4. Rotate API keys, tokens and service credentials on schedule and immediately on any staff exit.
5. Run a phishing simulation and short security training for every staff member with admin access, tracking who clicks, who reports, and who needs a repeat.
6. Confirm any platform SOC or PCI claim before it is repeated, and maintain the hosted-versus-self-hosted responsibility map.

## Checks
- Offboarding is confirmed, never assumed complete.
- DMARC's exact policy state (none, quarantine, reject) is stated, not summarized as 'set up'.
- Every admin-access staff member has a tracked training result.

## Output
The requested pillar's result, rolled into the quarterly security scorecard with a named owner per pillar.

## Example
A staff member who left 2 months ago still has an active API key; the credential rotation check catches it and the fix list names the exact key to revoke today, not at the next scheduled rotation.

# Confirm PCI DSS scope and complete the SAQ

## Purpose
Keep raw card data out of the brand's own systems and complete the right self-assessment questionnaire for the flow that actually exists.

## Steps
1. Map exactly how checkout takes payment: a gateway-hosted field, a redirect, or a direct API integration.
2. Determine which SAQ type applies to that exact flow, not the type the gateway's marketing suggests.
3. Confirm with a live checkout trace that raw card data never touches the brand's own servers outside the confirmed scope.
4. Complete the SAQ's factual items from the confirmed scope and flow.
5. Flag any item needing a signature or a third-party attestation for a person to complete.

## Checks
- Scope is confirmed by tracing a live checkout, not by reading settings alone.
- No signature or attestation is provided by this skill; submission stays with a person.

## Output
The payment flow map, the applicable SAQ type, the scope confirmation, and the completed SAQ draft.

## Example
A checkout believed to be fully hosted by the gateway is found, on a live trace, to pass a card's last 4 digits through the brand's own order confirmation email template; the scope confirmation flags this before the SAQ is finalized.

# Correlate account-takeover signals across systems

## Purpose
A single system's own alert stays quiet when a login looks normal to it; this skill compares the same person's logins across every admin-level system at once.

## Steps
1. Pull login geography, device and time from Shopify admin, the ad accounts, the ESP and the payment processor.
2. Match login events for the same person across at least 2 systems within a short time window.
3. Flag any sequence where geography or device differs from that person's normal pattern, even if each individual system's own alert stayed quiet.
4. Rank the flag by the worst action that account could take: change payment settings, move ad budget, or export customer data.

## Checks
- A match requires the same person's account across at least 2 systems, not one system's activity alone.
- The ranking states the specific worst action available to that account, not just that a login looked unusual.

## Output
Matched login sequences, anomaly flags, and a ranked exposure list.

## Example
An admin logs into Shopify from a new city at 2am, then into the ad account from the same new city 40 minutes later; the correlation flags it as high exposure because that admin account can move ad budget.
